articles.content: Legora can’t read a single trace of what its agent does for a lawyer. The data belongs to the law firm’s clients. How do you build and test an agent when you can’t see its work? Jacob Lauritzen is the CTO of Legora, one of the fastest-growing companies in legal tech history. The team started in a Stockholm basement with ChatGPT, Swedish law, and a search tool. Today, a lawyer can use Legora to draft and edit Word documents, review 10,000 contracts in a single table, or run due diligence. The agent also coordinates work between lawyers, clients, and other agents. When Legora made its own acquisitions, the team used it for diligence. What we talked about • Why Legora resisted adding a model picker for years, and why it finally added one • Jacob’s estimate that models already do about 60% of legal work well, and why the rest takes a smarter model • How three engineers and three lawyers build test environments modeled on customers’ work, much like the “worlds” used in reinforcement learning • A citation problem where the model got it right 70% of the time, then 99% after one release. Legora didn’t have to change anything. • Why Legora runs everything on Azure and why it doesn’t use ElevenLabs • Tabular Review, the million-cell spreadsheet the industry copied down to the name • How intake works, how agents create lists, and how a list can start another agent • What legal engineers and forward-deployed engineers each do, and who gets to write code • The 300 Spartans slide Jacob used to argue that 20 engineers would be enough forever. Now there are 100, and he still feels short-handed. • Why Jacob finds Fable and Opus too chatty for drafting and likes Astra’s concise writing • Why drafting a long contract is a search problem • Whether model labs will cut off legal tools the way they cut off coding tools • What happens to law firm partnerships, the billable hour, and jobs for junior lawyers Legora is hiring engineers in New York, Stockholm, and London. articles.content: When a developer gives an AI agent a coding task, the agent does more than answer once. It plans, generates code, runs tests, and repeats the process to correct errors. A single task can use 10 to 50 times more tokens than a basic chat prompt. The more useful the agent becomes, the more calls it makes. With per-token pricing, the workflows creating the most value can also become the most expensive. The financial pressure is already visible. Uber reportedly exhausted its entire 2026 AI budget by April after expanding its use of Claude Code. GitHub Copilot moved from flat-rate pricing to metered credits. Gartner predicts that AI coding token costs will surpass average developer salaries by 2028. The natural response is rationing usage caps, seat limits, and approvals before developers launch agents. But blanket limits can restrict the workflows delivering value. They also optimize the wrong number. Cost per token measures consumption, not results. Some spending reflects waste, including retries and runaway loops. Some represents the work of shipping software. A meter cannot distinguish them, and neither can a spending cap. Measure the software that ships A better measure is cost per merged pull request: total AI-assisted development cost divided by the number of changes that pass review and are merged. Track rework and defects alongside it so cheaper changes do not conceal lower quality. If that cost falls as AI usage rises, without compromising quality, developers are converting more consumption into useful software. The question is not how many tokens they use, but how much finished work the investment produces. Improving that equation requires two changes: reserve expensive inference for tasks that need it, and lower the cost of routine work. Match the model to the task Agentic coding does not require the most powerful model at every step. Use a frontier model, or an on-premises flagship when policy requires it, for difficult planning and novel reasoning. Route suitable work, including code generation, test creation, and repeated refactoring, to open-weight models you operate yourself. A gateway can route requests according to task complexity, data sensitivity, cost, and latency. This reserves premium inference for the moments that justify it rather than applying premium pricing to an entire workflow. Meter the exception, not the workload. Open-weight models make this division increasingly practical. Software-engineering benchmarks show that leading open-weight models can approach frontier performance on some tasks. That does not establish equivalence across every repository or workflow. Evaluate candidates against your own code, tests, and acceptance criteria before assigning production work. Change the economics of repeated use Next, decide who owns the capacity. With rented inference, every call adds to the bill. With owned capacity, most of the cost is committed upfront, so each additional call gets cheaper as usage grows. The economics are simple: per-token pricing makes heavy use more expensive, while owned capacity becomes more efficient as teams use it more. Ownership is not free, though. Power, operations, maintenance, and depreciation all must be considered. The number that matters is the fully loaded cost per merged pull request. Owned capacity also delivers a type of value that never appears on an invoice: control over sensitive code. When code generation and testing run on-premises, proprietary code stays inside the enterprise. Only approved planning prompts and governed exceptions go to external models, through a gateway the organization controls. That opens the sensitive repositories where security usually stalls adoption, and where the biggest gains are waiting. Test the operating model At HPE, a hybrid AI platform routes routine workloads from more than 150 internal applications to open-weight models running on premises, including on HPE Private Cloud AI. The result: token costs down 30 to 50%. That is the point of hybrid. With HPE Private Cloud AI, owning your inference does not mean giving up frontier models. Run the volume on capacity you own and let a gateway send the hardest work. Data also shows that usage, not licensed headcount, drives spend. The top 5% of users generated most of the consumption, and the heaviest used roughly 450 times more than the lightest on the same license. If power users grow from a small minority to half the workforce, monthly spend can rise about 4.4 times with flat headcount. Your mix will differ, which is exactly why you need to measure it. HPE tracks two metrics and recommends customers do the same. First, it tracks cost per active developer, because averaging across all licenses hides the power users driving spend. Second, it tracks cost per merged pull request, because it connects AI spending to software that ships. Baseline both costs before changing infrastructure. Then run a complete development cycle on owned capacity. If both metrics do not improve as usage grows, your current model may still be the better choice. Build for adoption, not rationing Owned capacity is not for everyone. Low or unpredictable usage favors APIs, with no capital tied up in idle infrastructure. Ownership pays off when sustained demand keeps it busy. Most enterprises will run hybrid: frontier APIs for demanding or intermittent work, owned capacity for repeatable volume. A governed gateway decides what leaves the building, so you get frontier models without giving up sovereignty over your code. As developers lean harder on coding agents, usage will keep rising. The real choice is whether that growth shows up as a bigger variable-cost bill or as more software shipped on capacity you own. The companies that lead AI-assisted development will not ration adoption to control costs. They will build an operating model where more AI use improves the economics instead of undermining them. articles.content: In 2001, a decade after he invented the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision. Together with two colleagues, he published an article in the magazine Scientific American in which he outlined what he called the “Semantic Web” : an internet designed to be navigated by autonomous software agents that could address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves. To illustrate what this might look like, Berners-Lee and his colleagues told a story about a pair of siblings who use their agents to automatically research and book physical therapy appointments for their mother, making sure they would be covered by insurance and fit their busy calendars. At the turn of the millennium, this vision seemed far-fetched: Google had only been online for a couple of years, and most people were still on dial-up connections. But a quarter-century on, the dream of autonomous software agents that use the internet and carry out tasks for us has finally been realized. New tools such as Meta’s blockbuster Muse agent, OpenAI’s Dots, and Anthropic’s Claude Duet are being given access to people’s email inboxes and bank accounts, Meanwhile, in a series of worrying incidents, agents created by OpenAI broke free of their sandboxes and caused havoc online. Just as the rise of smartphones sparked the development of a more atomized and attention-grabbing internet, the advent of powerful AI systems heralds a new era: We’re facing not the semantic web but the agentic web. This new web is developing out of sight and in ways that might not be entirely within our control. As it grows, the agentic web will inevitably transform the human web—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess. For Berners-Lee’s original vision to work, internet users would have had to annotate the pages they built with special tags so that a software agent could understand each element’s meaning—say, “street address” for the part of a physical therapy office’s web page that indicates its location and “appointment types” for the list of services. And so the idea never really caught on. “It’s a lot of labor,” says Eni Mustafaraj, a professor of computer science at Wellesley College. “And the benefits of that were not obvious.” For the next two decades, then, the internet remained a place that put humans first, with the odd Twitter reply bot or web scraper to round things out. Large language models changed that. Unlike the agents that Berners-Lee was imagining, today’s LLM-based agents don’t need any tags to understand which part of the text on a clinic’s site is its address and which details the services it offers. They can search for and process text far faster than any human, and agents with multimodal capabilities can even interpret screenshots of websites and click on specific elements such as hyperlinks and drop-down menus. They’re also just a way more intuitive means of finding information and accomplishing tasks online. Rather than poring over pages of Google results to find a budget-friendly product dupe or a half-remembered meme, why not have Claude or ChatGPT peruse dozens of sites in just a few minutes, guided only by your vague query? Or go one step further and use a personal assistant agent like Muse to hunt down a restaurant reservation or book a flight. As agents flood online spaces, this new user base is changing the web for good. Time magazine, for instance, is publishing versions of its articles that are easier for agents to parse and has started selling ads targeted at them. Companies from Etsy to Expedia have partnered with the major AI firms to build tools that allow agents to interface seamlessly with their services. Despite these early efforts, it’s still tough to tell exactly what forms the agentic web will take and how it will change our online experience. Depending on how it’s designed and who controls access to it, we could be in for something that’s as open and customizable as the web of the early 2000s, only far easier to use. Alternatively, we could be reduced to viewing much of the web through tiny portholes controlled by a few dominant platforms, as independent sites and creators struggle to survive the shift. And as this summer’s series of OpenAI security incidents suggests, the agents might even build their own online networks and resources—whether we want them to or not. How this plays out also depends on us: which parts of our online lives we’re happy to delegate to our agents and where we will still demand a human-centric internet. “There’s a lot we don’t know yet about how users want to use [agents],” says Ajit Varma, head of Firefox at Mozilla. But whatever does happen, the changes will be big. “It’s probably on par with getting a mobile phone,” he says. “I think things are going to change very dramatically.” Building a web for agents There are two ways to approach building the agentic web. The first involves training agents to use browsers like humans—scrolling, clicking, typing—and letting them loose on the web that we’re all used to. The second requires building tools that allow agents to interface with the internet via text and code, their preferred media. That possibility offers more separation between the human and the agentic web: designers can create different experiences for those who use text commands and those who use browsers. When Siva Reddy, a professor of computer science and linguistics at McGill University, began studying LLM agents in 2024, he focused on the first option. “At that time, we thought it should be that the best agent in the world is probably an agent that can use a browser,” he says. Such an agent would integrate seamlessly with the preexisting human web, and its owner could easily supervise it by watching as it navigated familiar interfaces. The frontier AI companies were already developing these “computer-use agents.” But they didn’t work terribly well—at least not at first.

The Series E and F rounds combined $1.65 billion in funding. The surge comes amid soaring demand for AI inference services, with Fal surpassing $800 million in annualized revenue earlier this year. Companies in the inference sector, including Baseten and Fireworks AI, are also growing rapidly despite thin gross margins due to high compute costs.

articles.content: A local-first app is only local-first if it survives a cut mid-request. Most survive a cut between requests. The difference is one open socket and one blocked write. Start with the real failure. A user hits save while the network dies. Your code awaits a fetch that never resolves. The spinner runs for thirty seconds, then the offline banner appears. That banner is a status indicator. It is not a fallback path. The fallback is the branch that must run when the promise never settles. You cannot review that branch by reading code. You have to make the wire fail on command. A stub that fails on four ways I do not test this against a real provider. Real providers fail politely and rarely. A stub fails on schedule, in the exact shape you choose. Here is a stdlib-only HTTP stub, no dependencies, four modes. Place it in faultstub.py . # python faultstub.py --mode truncate --after 40 --port 8787 import argparse , json , time from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler , HTTPServer MODE = { " name " : " ok " , " after " : 40 , " stall " : 5.0 } class Handler ( BaseHTTPRequestHandler ): protocol_version = " HTTP/1.1 " def do_POST ( self ): n = int ( self . headers . get ( " content-length " , 0 )) body = self . rfile . read ( n ) payload = json . dumps ({ " ok " : True , " bytes " : len ( body )}). encode () mode = MODE [ " name " ] if mode == " reset " : # connection dies before headers self . connection . close () return if mode == " stall " : # headers arrive, body never does time . sleep ( MODE [ " stall " ]) if mode == " truncate " : # 200 + short body, then close self . send_response ( 200 ) self . send_header ( " content-length " , str ( len ( payload ) + 64 )) self . end_headers () self . wfile . write ( payload [: MODE [ " after " ]]) self . connection . close () return self . send_response ( 200 ) self . send_header ( " content-type " , " application/json " ) self . send_header ( " content-length " , str ( len ( payload ))) self . end_headers () self . wfile . write ( payload ) def log_message ( self , fmt , * args ): print ( MODE [ " name " ], self . path , flush = True ) if __name__ == " __main__ " : p = argparse . ArgumentParser () p . add_argument ( " --mode " , default = " ok " , choices = [ " ok " , " truncate " , " stall " , " reset " ]) p . add_argument ( " --after " , type = int , default = 40 ) p . add_argument ( " --stall " , type = float , default = 5.0 ) p . add_argument ( " --port " , type = int , default = 8787 ) a = p . parse_args () MODE . update ( name = a . mode , after = a . after , stall = a . stall ) HTTPServer (( " 127.0.0.1 " , a . port ), Handler ). serve_forever () Now run your client against it. Point API_BASE at the stub and sweep all four modes. for m in ok truncate stall reset ; do echo "== mode: $m " python faultstub.py --mode " $m " --port 8787 & STUB_PID = $! API_BASE = http://127.0.0.1:8787 python client.py --runs 20 kill $STUB_PID wait $STUB_PID 2>/dev/null done The interesting mode is truncate . The server returns 200 and half a body. A naive client parses it, throws, and reports success to the UI. That is the bug this drill exists to find. Three assertions, not a vibe A drill without assertions is a demo. Fix three invariants before you run anything, and fail loudly when one breaks. assert p99_local_write_ms < 50 , " local write blocked on the wire " assert outbox . depth () == submitted , " queued item lost " assert len ( sent_ids ) == len ( set ( sent_ids )), " duplicate send after retry " Pick your own millisecond budget. Fifty is a proposal, not a measurement. The point is that the number is written down before the test, not after it. The duplicate assertion matters most. Every retry path invents a second send. Without an idempotency key generated before the first attempt, reset mode will quietly double-write. Sort each call into a class The drill gives you facts per call site. Map every outbound call to one of three classes before you decide where it runs. class offline requirement expected verdict local write (save, edit) commits under budget, always LOCAL-OK cacheable read (list, profile) serves last known value LOCAL-OK on cache hit enrichment (summarize, tag, suggest) may fail, may retry later CLOUD-ONLY If a "local write" returns LOCAL-DEGRADED under stall , you do not have a local-first app. You have a cache with a marketing name. Fix the write path first. Enrichment is the opposite case. Nobody closes the tab because a tag arrives four seconds late. That class tolerates cold starts, queueing, and retries. It also tolerates running somewhere you do not own. Where a free server actually wins A free server wins on one property. It wins when the class is stateless, bursty, and tolerant of latency you did not choose. Enrichment is exactly that shape. The client sends text, gets a label back, and the result is nice-to-have. Nothing in that loop needs a warm local runtime. Nothing needs to survive a partition. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

articles.title: Cut the Wire Mid-Request: Prove the Offline Path
articles.headline: Stub simulates network cut to expose local-first app bugs
articles.summary: A developer tool simulates network failures to test local-first apps. The 'truncate' mode returns 200 with a partial body, causing naive clients to report success while losing data. Three assertions verify local write timing, queue depth, and duplicate sends. The drill maps outbound calls into classes: local writes must commit under budget, while enrichment tasks tolerate latency. A free server wins when handling stateless, bursty workloads tolerant of chosen latency.

articles.content: This October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier. This is more commits than GitHub received in all of 2025. Chances are, you’re generating more code than you were a year ago. But ask yourself: do you feel 400% more productive than you were last year? Building software takes more than a good prompt. As AI speeds up implementation, software developers are feeling more pressure in other places: a Faros AI study found that pull requests spent 441% longer in review when teams went from low to high AI adoption. As a software developer, you gather requirements and steer implementation, review changes and evaluate test results, then investigate what happens in production. Agents can help you work more efficiently across all of these stages: Plan, Build, Verify, and Observe. We’ll walk through what an effective agentic engineering workflow looks like on GitHub. Plan: Get everyone and every agent on the same page See if this sounds familiar. You’re planning an API change. The design is in one tool, a compatibility requirement is buried in Slack, and an old pull request explains why the current implementation works this way. Before you can write a useful plan, you need to connect those details, compare approaches, and agree on how existing clients will keep working. What looked like a straightforward planning task has become hours of searching, cross-checking, and chasing answers. You’re exhausted before implementation even begins. You can use Copilot to pull that scattered context into one place, work through the tradeoffs, and turn the decisions into an implementation plan. Plan together where your team already works. Use Copilot in Slack or Teams to collaborate with everyone involved—from product managers and designers to analysts and business stakeholders. Bring in context from connected tools so your team can check assumptions, contribute ideas, and refine requirements together. Turn agreed-upon requirements into actionable work. Ask Copilot to create GitHub Issues with the context and acceptance criteria needed for implementation, breaking out tasks that can be handled separately. Keep routine triage from consuming planning time. Use GitHub Agentic Workflows to label your issues and estimate task complexity. Assign low-complexity tasks directly to Copilot, then spend your time focusing on harder decisions. Give complex work the planning it needs. Use Plan Mode in your preferred Copilot surface to compare approaches and refine an implementation plan. Review and approve the plan before handing it off to Copilot to begin implementation. What took days of searching and context gathering now produces a reviewable plan, explicit acceptance criteria, and scoped issues, with your time spent on the decisions instead of the retrieval. Then, once you settle on an approach, you’ve already set yourself and your agents up to implement your plan. Build: Move more than one task forward at a time You’re ready to turn that plan into code. But life has other ideas. Your agent is halfway through a task, your next meeting starts in five minutes, and your dog has been staring at the door for twenty. Then someone in the meeting points out an edge case the implementation needs to handle. Everyone needs something from you at once. You’d like to keep making progress, but you can’t be in three places at the same time. You can keep your work moving without being tied to the computer where you started it. Continue your conversation from another device. Session continuity lets you pick up the same Copilot session across clients, so you can work wherever it’s most convenient for you. Let work continue after you close your laptop. Copilot runs tasks in cloud sandboxes , keeping execution off your machine and allowing you to leave and return to a session later. Work on separate tasks without mixing their edits. The Copilot app gives sessions isolated copies of the repository, so an implementation task and a documentation update don’t share an unfinished working tree. Carry project knowledge into each task. Repository instructions capture conventions and validation commands, while shared memory stores useful facts Copilot can reuse across a repository. Copilot Dreaming reviews eligible sessions and pull request feedback to keep memories current and propose instruction or skill updates. That means less time re-explaining how your team works and more consistent help from Copilot across tasks. Match the models to the work. Select Copilot Fusion to choose models and reasoning depth for the task, bringing in additional models to review a solution when needed. You set the effort level to balance quality, cost, and response time. Follow company rules wherever you work. Enterprise managed settings carry your company’s policies and configured tools across Copilot surfaces, reducing setup differences as you move between clients. Writing code is more than shooting off a single prompt to your LLM and seeing what you get back. And with more work on your plate than ever, it can be difficult to maintain your coding standards and deliver your projects on time. Copilot helps tasks progress independently with shared project knowledge, while letting you pick up a session where you left off across devices. That gives you more room to work through implementation decisions and handle changes as they come up. And as your work finishes, you have focused changes ready to review. Verify: Spend your attention where it counts After spending an hour wrangling your agents to get them moving in the right direction, you think you’ve all landed in a good spot. So you open a pull request labeled “small refactor.” It changes 47 files. You wanted feedback on shared validation logic, but it’s buried among updates to every endpoint that calls it, formatting changes, and several hundred lines of generated tests. You wonder how long it will take to get an approval on this, given the endless list of pull requests on your team’s review board. That review queue is the 441% in practice.

articles.title: Beyond code generation: A developer’s guide to agentic engineering

articles.summary: GitHub Blog reports that in October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier, exceeding the total commits received in all of 2025. The article explores how AI tools like GitHub Copilot support agentic engineering workflows across planning, building, verification, and observation, while noting that increased AI adoption has led to pull requests spending 441% longer in review. It addresses developer productivity challenges, the need for human judgment in AI-assisted development, and GitHub's efforts to improve secret detection and developer workflows.

articles.content: Dacă citești asta, probabil ai chiar acum peste 40 de file deschise. Chrome consumă 4 GB de RAM, ventilatorul laptopului urlă și nu găsești fila pe care ai deschis-o acum 20 de minute. Am construit Tabs in One exact pentru asta. Problema Bara de file din Chrome este o bandă orizontală. Imediat ce ai mai mult de ~10 file, acestea se micșorează în fâșii minuscule. Pierzi evidența a ce este deschis, duplicatele se adună, iar consumul de RAM crește. Managerii de file există, dar majoritatea fie: adaugă încă o bară laterală care concurează cu conținutul tău, fie cer cont / abonament pentru funcții de bază, fie sunt abandonate. Ce face Tabs in One Tabs in One adună toate filele deschise într-o singură pagină curată, cu o singură coloană . Când îl pornești, fiecare filă deschisă este mutată pe acea pagină, iar filele originale se închid — RAM-ul se eliberează imediat. Poți readuce orice filă (sau toate) ca file normale cu un singur clic, fără să pierzi nimic. Funcții principale: Vizualizare pe o singură coloană — fiecare filă ca un rând lizibil cu titlu și URL, fără favicon-uri minuscule. Restaurare cu un clic — readu filele individual sau pe toate deodată. Doar linkuri unice — dacă pagina managerului este deja deschisă, se adaugă doar linkurile unice noi. Nimic nu se pierde, fără duplicate. Backup-uri — backup automat zilnic (ultimele 5 păstrate), plus „fă backup acum” manual. Export / Import — JSON sau HTML, ca să muți lista de file între calculatoare. Statistici și ranguri — file salvate, RAM eliberat, record personal. Ranguri gamificate de la „Neat Tabber” la „Final Boss of RAM”. Împărtășește-ți recordul — generează o imagine și un link de partajat. Cum funcționează Apasă pe pictograma Tabs in One (sau folosește meniul contextual: „Open Tabs in One”). Toate filele se mută pe o pagină cu o singură coloană; originalele se închid și RAM-ul se eliberează. Răsfoiește, caută sau restaurează oricând vrei. Permisiuni folosite: tabs , storage , contextMenus , alarms . Fără cont, fără abonament, niciun fel de date nu părăsesc browserul tău. Dezavantaje oneste Are nevoie de permisiunea tabs pentru a citi și gestiona filele — acesta este chiar scopul, dar unii utilizatori sunt precauți. Codul este deschis spre verificare. Dacă te bazezi pe faptul că filele fixate rămân fixate, verifică mai întâi comportamentul la restaurare. Este un manager de file, nu un instrument de sincronizare a sesiunilor — nu sincronizează între dispozitive (folosește export/import pentru asta). Instalare Chrome Web Store: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/ehghdjiblhadojkedfjkmbeohiphogdb Gratuit. Nu necesită cont. Pentru cine este Cercetători și autori cu peste 30 de file de referință. Dezvoltatori care jonglează cu documentație, Stack Overflow și GitHub. Oricine căruia consumul de RAM al Chrome îi face ventilatorul laptopului să urle. Încearcă o săptămână. Dacă nu îți economisește timp, dezinstalează — cost zero. Construit cu Chrome Manifest V3. Feedback-ul este binevenit. Also published at https://tabsinone.wordpress.com/2026/11/07/tabs-in-one-strange-toate-filele-chrome-intr-o-singura-coloana-si-elibereaza-ram/

articles.headline: Tabs in One consolidates Chrome tabs into a single column to free RAM
articles.summary: Tabs in One aggregates all open Chrome tabs into a single-column page, closing original tabs to immediately free RAM. The extension addresses Chrome's tab overflow issue where exceeding ~10 tabs reduces them to tiny icons, causing users to lose track and increasing memory use. It offers one-click restoration, unique link-only saving, daily backups, and export/import functionality. The tool is free, requires no account, and targets users managing 30+ reference tabs or developers juggling multiple documents.

articles.content: The highest priorities for the transition to post-quantum cryptography are the basic building blocks of authenticated key-agreement protocols such as TLS. Without these building blocks in place, secure communication on the Internet will not be possible once cryptographically relevant quantum computers come online. However, today we rely on quantum-vulnerable cryptography for much more than TLS. Privacy Pass is a protocol used by site operators like Cloudflare to help protect applications from abuse. One way we do this is by rate limiting individual clients so that no one client consumes too many of the site's resources. Normally this involves some combination of friction or loss of privacy for users: CAPTCHAs or other challenges to moderate traffic, along with accounts and fingerprinting to identify traffic.Privacy Pass was designed to avoid this tradeoff between friction and privacy. The basic idea is that a client gets issued a number of tokens , which they can redeem in exchange for access to the site. Crucially, each token is unlinkable to the client it was issued to, ensuring the client can use the site as they always had without sacrificing privacy. With 10 years of deployment experience under our belts — using Privacy Pass for applications such as privacy proxies (like iCloud Private Relay) and relays (like Privacy Gateway) — we, along with others , are collaborating to bring the next generation of this technology to the web. One of our goals is to develop more sophisticated tools for managing agentic traffic that would otherwise consume too many resources and degrade performance for human visitors. Another goal is to foster a more open ecosystem by making it easier for more types of clients to participate. Achieving these goals requires developing new capabilities beyond what Privacy Pass offers today. Given the trajectory, in this post we look at the prospects for post-quantum. In fact, we're in better shape than one might think. Privacy Pass still relies on classical cryptography, like RSA and elliptic curves. This means that a quantum attacker will be able to forge tokens at will and use them to bypass whatever security mechanism the site operator wants to implement (such as rate limiting). On the other hand, Privacy Pass is unconditionally private, meaning no attacker, quantum or not, can link the redemption of a token to its issuance. What's more, the new capabilities we're developing for this new generation of private authentication technology can and will be instantiated in a way that upholds the same guarantee: your interaction remains private even after Q-day. This gives us a little breathing room, but we will need an alternative soon. This is an active area of research that has made significant strides in recent years. Still, just as is the case with other aspects of the transition, the primary challenge is the sheer size of post-quantum alternatives: ML-DSA-44 signatures are a whopping 2,420 bytes, while ECDSA-P256 signatures are just 64 bytes. And there's not much hope for drop-in replacements any time soon. Just as for TLS, we'll have to settle for primitives with higher cost and re-engineer our systems to bear this cost . But what will those primitives be? In this post, we'll explore one potential future for post-quantum privacy on the web, made possible by a recent breakthrough in the design of blind signatures. What we need to build: a brief look at MOLE Let's start with an overview of this new technology, which is presently called MOLE ("Moderation Of unLinkable Endorsements"). We'll have much more to say about MOLE later on, but for now we'll highlight the details that are most relevant to cryptography. One of the core components of Privacy Pass is a blind signature scheme, which allows a client to obtain a signature under an issuer's secret key without revealing to the issuer the message that it signed. The client can then reveal the message and blind signature later on without linking the signature to its issuance. One type of Privacy Pass token consists of the message and blindly issued signature. To verify the token, the verifier needs the issuer's public key, and so necessarily learns the identity of the issuer. Thus while these tokens protect the identity of the client, they don't protect the identity of the issuer. Of course, this is exactly what we want for some use cases. The identity of the issuer tells us something about what type of client is connecting to our edge, a signal we use to make decisions in some of our products and for some of our customers. For instance, a client might use a token issued by one of our customers to prove it is authorized to use the customer's VPN product. However, for many use cases, this is more information than we actually need to make a decision to grant a client access to a resource. Normally we only care that the token was issued by some entity we trust. In fact, MOLE takes this a step further: the token should hide the identity of the issuer altogether so that we can't treat tokens differently based on who issued them. This guarantees equal treatment regardless of the type of client, making it easier for more clients to participate. This issuer-hiding property is achieved through a new object called an endorsement . An endorsement is issued by an anchor and redeemed by a moderator . Before redemption, the client and moderator agree on an anchor set , the public keys of the anchors trusted by the moderator. During redemption, the client proves it was issued an endorsement by one of the anchors in the anchor set without revealing which one. Upon acceptance, the moderator issues the client the MOLE credential it will use to moderate the client's interaction with the site. An endorsement can take many forms, but its key property is that it can be redeemed while hiding the identity of the anchor that issued it.
articles.excerpt: The highest priorities for the transition to post-quantum cryptography are the basic building blocks of authenticated key-agreement protocols such as TLS. Without these building blocks in place, secure communication on the Internet will not be possible once cryptographically relevant quantum computers come online. However, today we rely on quantum-vulnerable cryptography for much more than TLS.
articles.title: The post-quantum future of web privacy
articles.headline: Cloudflare explores post-quantum privacy with MOLE blind signature breakthrough
articles.summary: Cloudflare discusses transitioning Privacy Pass to post-quantum cryptography. The new MOLE protocol aims to hide issuer identity while enabling adaptable, efficient credentials. Researchers highlight a breakthrough in blind signatures that could allow post-quantum security without sacrificing privacy, though larger signature sizes present system re-engineering challenges.

articles.content: I’m a CS junior, and I’m in the middle of building this, not at the start of it. There’s a specific kind of tired that comes from being the scheduler. A chat window for the code, a tab for the docs, a terminal agent for the build. None of them know about each other, so you’re the wire between them, all day. One night I closed my laptop with everything half finished. The next morning it was all still there, waiting for me to reconnect it. Work only existed while I was looking at it. So I built a place for it to live. SHADOW is a platform where you deploy agents. Each has its own chat, model, permissions and schedule, and runs on your own PC with your own keys. You give an agent a goal, not six instructions. It writes a plan first, and you approve it, which is where you catch a misunderstanding while it’s still cheap. Then it works inside the folders you granted and asks before anything risky, showing the exact command. Then it reports what it did and what’s queued. The first version minimised my editor mid-sentence to reach something behind it. I was annoyed, and that annoyance became the whole product. Each agent now gets only the folders you pick, only the commands you see first, and a separate browser profile. Screen control can only be started by you. Nothing an agent reads can widen its permissions, and system folders and credential stores stay blocked. The morning after, the reports were finished. I answered the two things that needed me and got on with real work. Windows 11, on the Microsoft Store, free, no account. What would you hand over tonight, if it didn’t mean explaining it twice? https://tryshadow.vercel.app/ https://apps.microsoft.com/detail/9P52N15720DG

articles.headline: CS student launches SHADOW platform for autonomous AI agents
articles.summary: A computer science junior built SHADOW, a platform that lets users deploy autonomous AI agents on their own PC. Each agent operates within selected folders and permissions, writes a plan for user approval before acting, and reports completed tasks. The tool aims to reduce context-switching fatigue by letting AI handle multi-step workflows locally without cloud accounts.

articles.content: An agent can prepare a change without being allowed to make it. That distinction is the simplest way to get useful automation into an enterprise workflow while keeping a person accountable for consequential actions. Consider a supplier onboarding assistant. It reads a request, checks whether mandatory fields are present, compares the supplier against an approved registry, and prepares an ERP record. It must not create the supplier or release a payment on its own. The approval step belongs between prepare and execute , not as a polite question the model asks after it has already called the write API. Split the workflow into explicit states A practical state machine is received → validated → proposed → awaiting_review → approved/rejected → executed → reconciled . Persist the proposal and its source references before asking for approval. An approver should see the original request, the exact fields to be written, the evidence used, uncertainty, and any policy warnings. The approval decision should refer to a versioned proposal ID, so an edited proposal cannot inherit an earlier approval. The write operation should be a separate service endpoint. Give the agent read access and permission to create a proposal, while the execution service accepts only a valid approval token from the workflow system. A prompt such as “always ask before writing” is helpful guidance, but it is not an access control. Make approval specific “Looks good” is too vague. Ask the reviewer to approve the exact action: create supplier S-1042 with the displayed bank and tax details, or send the displayed reply to a named recipient. Show a diff against the current record. Let the reviewer edit, reject or escalate. For financial, identity, personal-data or regulated decisions, the appropriate reviewer and evidence may differ; encode those rules outside the model. A minimal approval record contains the proposal ID and version, actor identity, action type, target system, payload hash, reviewer identity, decision, timestamp, reason, and execution result. Set an expiry and do not reuse the approval for a later attempt with a changed payload. Handle failures after the click Approval is not proof that the write succeeded. The executor needs an idempotency key so a retry does not create two suppliers. Record the target system's response and reconcile it with the intended change. If execution fails, leave the item in an exception queue rather than asking the model to invent a recovery path. Test the rejected, expired, modified, duplicate and unavailable-system paths before a pilot. Microsoft's Agent Framework documentation describes a related pattern: an approval-required tool pauses the workflow and emits a request that an external reviewer can approve or reject. The exact SDK is optional; the durable pause and the separate authorisation boundary are the important parts. Start small: choose one low-volume workflow, one write action and one reviewer group. Measure time from proposal to decision, reviewer corrections, false positives, and failed executions. Those measures tell you whether the agent reduced work or merely moved it to the approval queue. I work at OneBonsAI Gulf. For teams planning a bounded agent with human oversight, see our agentic AI implementation service . Further reading: Microsoft Agent Framework human-in-the-loop workflows .

articles.content: Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we’ve been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running. Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our first post in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our last post , we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage. We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the reference update, and a reference update is tiny in comparison. Virtual replicas were the first step toward building around that, and the means by which we onboard repositories to the new architecture. The rest of the architecture builds on that observation. Only reference updates need agreement. That lets the parts of Git infrastructure that used to be tightly coupled (storing data, serving requests, and maintaining repositories) scale independently. For developers, Git stays Git: they push, fetch, and branch the same way, with the same protections in place. Below, we walk through the requirements behind the design, follow a request through the system, and dive deep into two of its components. Building for agent scale We think about the scale of the GitHub platform along two axes: Horizontal scale is how many developers and agents can work across many repositories. Many of GitHub’s current approaches on this axis have been battle-tested over the years and are carried forward to the new architecture: partitioning of tenants across infrastructure, isolation and/or fairness enforcement of tenant traffic, and load-aware routing, to name a few. Vertical scale is how many developers and agents can work on one repository. As agents write more code, we expect individual repositories to get larger and busier, so most of our requirements came from the vertical axis. Today, the busiest repositories on GitHub.com receive at most dozens of writes in a single second, typically in short bursts. As more of that work shifts to agents running in parallel and around the clock, we expect those bursts to become a sustained rate within the next year. Each push leads to more reads: CI runs, deployment systems pull the new commit, and other agents fetch it for context. This read fan-out results in a large amplification effect on overall traffic that scales with writes. We’re already seeing this trend play out on repositories at the top of the curve. The chart below shows daily requests to one repository on GitHub from March to May, when its traffic grew about 4x. Its growth has continued on an exponential trajectory since then. We have to plan for a world where agent-driven development keeps accelerating at this speed. Instead of planning for the next increment, we set a target of at least two orders of magnitude more scale. For a single repository, that meant the new architecture needed to: Accept thousands of writes per second. Support multiple writer nodes. There are two reasons for this: Experience has taught us that indexing incoming packs and checking object connectivity are the most CPU-expensive parts of a write, and that cost scales with the size of the write, so a single node will become compute-bound quickly. Spreading that work across many nodes improves fault tolerance and shortens recovery when a node fails. Minimize commit latency. An agent waits on each push before it moves to its next step. Record changes in order for each reference with the ability to quickly linearize across references. A virtual replica that falls behind needs to catch up by downloading only the data it needs to serve the incoming request. Keep reads cheap when nothing has changed, which is the common case given the read-to-write ratio. Let each component scale independently. On top of that, the system had to be able to improve overall reliability and scale globally. Introducing “Project Rubicon” In May of 2026, hot on the heels of the initial Azure migration, we started working on a design that could meet those demands. We tried several approaches. In all of them, pack data lived in Azure Blob Storage, and in some we experimented with keeping reference state there too. We’ll cover some of the trade-offs we found below, but we settled on a design we felt maximized throughput while preserving the correctness, durability, availability, and latency guarantees a platform like GitHub requires. We called it “Rubicon,” a nod to the point of no return the industry crossed with agentic development. Let’s walk through Rubicon from the top down. Many things stay the same: requests from Git clients, the API, and the web UI arrive at Spokes, which still handles routing and load balancing, and serves the internal API that the rest of GitHub uses to read and write repository data. Spokes also maintains its role as a placement and balancing service, maintaining the partitioning, isolation, and tenant fairness required for horizontal scale. The data plane underneath Spokes, in contrast, is new. Spokes routes each request to one of a small group of virtual replicas assigned to that repository. Virtual replicas are a single fleet of disposable compute that serves reads, writes, or both. A virtual replica’s local disk is a cache that can be rebuilt at any time.

articles.title: Inside GitHub’s new Git storage architecture
articles.headline: GitHub announces new storage architecture capable of 7,200 pushes per second
articles.summary: GitHub unveiled its new Git storage architecture at GitHub Universe, designed to support thousands of concurrent agents writing to repositories. Internal testing demonstrated the system can handle 7,200 pushes per second with consistently low read latency. The architecture decouples storage from compute and minimizes coordination, allowing reference updates to scale independently. This foundation aims to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers while maintaining Git's familiar workflow.

articles.content: AI Agents now act on the web for millions of people. To a Site, an Agent can take many forms. It may be indistinguishable from a human user carrying out a task, or it might look like one visitor carrying many Users. This removes the ability for the Site to recognize, serve, and hold accountable the user or users behind the Agent, and causes the Site to face the costs when something goes wrong. This post argues that in order for Sites to maximize the access they provide to Agents, the ecosystem must develop new mechanisms to preserve the relationship between Sites and Users. Traditionally, in Security and Fraud Prevention, that requires three things: Identity, Reputation, and Accountability, allowing Sites to answer: Is the person acting being truthful about who they are? Is that person trustworthy? And who answers for the action? “Personal AI Agents” (“Agents” for short) are automations that take instructions from a human (“User”) and pursue a goal by controlling a cloud computer or browser. They are usually hosted and maintained by an “Operator” as part of a managed service or consumer offering. Examples include Muse from Meta and dots from OpenAI, and more are launching all the time. Agents can potentially take any action online that their User could, without the limits that hold humans back. They don't tire, they run around the clock, they act in parallel, and they put up with friction no person would. Much of the web, from how Sites plan capacity to how they make money, assumes those limits. Fundamentally, remotely hosted Agents are intermediaries . An intermediary is anything that sits between a User and a Site, so the Site sees it instead of the User. Agents are the newest kind of intermediary, but intermediaries have existed for a long time. Cloud browsers (hosted browsers that software controls on a User's behalf) and Proxies (services that relay a User's traffic, including VPNs) are intermediaries too. What has changed is the trajectory. Agentic traffic is growing rapidly and may eclipse traditional human browsing on the Internet in the near future. This forces a reckoning for anyone operating a Site today. Historically, a Site could simply block intermediary traffic and require Users to disable the intermediary service. That stops working when the majority of traffic is agentic. Once blocking is no longer viable, Site Operators are left with the problem that intermediaries have always created. The Site loses direct information about the User and must decide whether to trust the intermediary without it. This post covers Agents hosted somewhere other than the User's device. Local agents (e.g. OpenClaw) or Agents running in the User's own browser, on their own device, are out of scope of the primary topic addressed by this post (see below, "On open source and local Agents"). This post rests on one principle: The Intermediation Principle : The business relationship between Users and Sites, and each participant’s security responsibilities, must be upheld regardless of intermediation. A Site needs new tools to recognize, serve, and hold accountable a User acting through an Agent just as it could if that User had visited directly. The Agent, and the Operator behind it, must be recognizable and accountable too, because an Agent can do what no User could. Agents are able to scale human access almost without limit, so they create new risks, even for behavior that was previously benign. The intermediary problem Meet Ezra. Ezra works as a personal assistant for people in her city. Her best client is Amy, a local CEO, but she also works for Bob, Charlie, and Debra. She runs their errands: groceries, appointments, paperwork, and flights. Ezra blends into the crowd. The corner grocer used to know Amy. He knew what she bought and set aside what he thought she'd like. Now only Ezra comes in, carrying orders for four people, and the grocer can't tell whose preferences are whose. He doesn't want to turn Ezra away, because she brings him a lot of business. Then Bob asks Ezra to buy him an iPhone. A week later he calls the store, says he never authorized the charge, and keeps the phone. To win the dispute, the store has to prove Bob asked for it. But the only person the store ever saw was Ezra. Then Charlie gives Ezra a list of passwords: "I forgot mine, but it's one of these." Ezra patiently tries each one at Charlie's bank. The bank can see an attack happening, but the only person it can ban is Ezra. Banning Ezra also bans Amy, Bob, and Debra. None of these business owners has a problem with Ezra herself. Their problem is that they can only see Ezra, not the person she's acting for. Swap Ezra for an AI Agent and the businesses for websites, and you have the web today. A website owner wants sufficient visibility both to prevent bad behavior and to effectively monetize or get value from their Site. But as with Ezra, much of that visibility goes away with AI Agents. Below is a list of actions that a website owner might want to address that were previously solved, but are made more challenging by allowing Agents. In nearly every challenge above, the Site bears the primary cost . That outcome follows from how trust works when an intermediary is involved. Our vision Our aim is an Internet where all Users have equal or greater access to websites than they had before. Before Agents, a Site was typically able to mitigate these risks with a collection of techniques, including fingerprinting the User’s device, session, and history. Users could still browse using private browsing mode, and we believe Agents should be able to do that as well. But they probably won’t be able to log in to a bank without additional verification. None of this requires an Agent to act like a human or a human to be present for every action.

articles.title: Agents aren’t humans (but they kinda are)
articles.headline: Cloudflare warns AI agents could eclipse human browsing, breaking site accountability
articles.summary: Cloudflare argues AI agents acting on the web for millions of users break site accountability by removing identity and reputation signals. As agent traffic grows, sites lose the ability to distinguish individual users, enforce age/geographic rules, prevent friendly fraud, or monetize content, as they can only see the agent, not the user behind it. The post calls for new mechanisms to preserve the user-site relationship as agentic traffic may soon eclipse traditional browsing.

articles.content: Spectre.Console uses square brackets for markup: [red]error[/] prints "error" in red. Any literal [ in your text has to be escaped as [[ , otherwise the parser tries to read it as a style. MarkupInterpolated and MarkupLineInterpolated exist so you don't have to think about that for values you interpolate. You write $"Hello {name}" and the library escapes name for you. Issue #1763 , opened by @yaakov-h , showed that this only worked when the value was a string . My fix is #2118 , merged on 12 May 2026 and released in 0.56.0 . The bug The issue's repro is short: class CoolThing { public override string ToString () => "This[contains, braces]." ; } AnsiConsole . MarkupLineInterpolated ( $"I have a { thing } " ); // InvalidOperationException: Could not find color or style 'contains,'. The detail I liked most in the report was the workaround. Calling {thing.ToString()} yourself avoids the crash, but the IDE then flags it with IDE0071, "simplify interpolation", because an explicit ToString() inside an interpolation hole is normally redundant. So the code the analyzer wants is the code that crashes. Where it came from All the interpolated APIs go through one method: internal static string EscapeInterpolated ( IFormatProvider provider , FormattableString value ) { object ?[] args = value . GetArguments (). Select ( arg => arg is string s ? s . EscapeMarkup () : arg ). ToArray (); return string . Format ( provider , value . Format , args ); } Strings are escaped. Everything else is handed to string.Format as it is, which calls ToString() on it later, after escaping has already happened. It doesn't take a contrived class to hit this. Plenty of ordinary .NET types have brackets in their default ToString() . I ran the same four calls against 0.55.0 and 0.56.0: var list = new List < int > { 1 , 2 , 3 }; // ToString(): System.Collections.Generic.List`1[System.Int32] int [] array = [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]; // ToString(): System.Int32[] var thing = new CoolThing (); // ToString(): This[contains, braces]. var when = new DateTime ( 2026 , 5 , 12 , 11 , 9 , 0 ); console . MarkupInterpolated ( $"items: { list } " ); console . MarkupInterpolated ( $"items: { array } " ); console . MarkupInterpolated ( $"value: { thing } " ); console . MarkupInterpolated ( $"at { when :[ HH : mm ]} " ); == 0.55.0 List<int> InvalidOperationException: Encountered malformed markup tag at position 54. int[] InvalidOperationException: Encountered malformed markup tag at position 21. custom ToString InvalidOperationException: Could not find color or style 'contains,'. DateTime with [..] format InvalidOperationException: Encountered malformed markup tag at position 10. == 0.56.0 List<int> ok int[] ok custom ToString ok DateTime with [..] format InvalidOperationException: Encountered malformed markup tag at position 10. The last line is intentional, and I'll come back to it. The fix internal static string EscapeInterpolated ( IFormatProvider provider , FormattableString value ) { object ?[] args = value . GetArguments () . Select ( arg => arg switch { null => null , string text => text . EscapeMarkup (), IFormattable => arg , _ => arg . ToString ()?. EscapeMarkup (), }) . ToArray (); return string . Format ( provider , value . Format , args ); } Each case is there for a reason: null stays null . Calling ToString() on it would throw, and turning it into an empty string early would hide it from a custom ICustomFormatter that wants to print something like <null> . There's a test for exactly that. string is escaped, as before. IFormattable is passed through untouched. This covers numbers, dates, Guid , TimeSpan and any type that understands format strings. If I converted these to strings early, {price:C} or {date:yyyy-MM-dd} would lose their format specifier, and culture-specific formatting through the provider would stop working. Their usual output doesn't contain brackets, so passing them through is the safe default. Everything else is converted with ToString() and escaped. That covers collections, arrays, records and your own classes. What this doesn't fix The IFormattable exception has a cost, and the last line of the experiment shows it. If a format string itself produces brackets, as in {when:[HH:mm]} , the output still reaches the markup parser unescaped. Fixing that would mean formatting each IFormattable with its format string and provider, then escaping the result. That's possible, but GetArguments() doesn't give you the per-hole format string. You would have to parse value.Format yourself, which is a much bigger change than the issue asked for. I left it out deliberately, and I'd rather say so here than pretend the problem is gone. If you need brackets from a format string, escape them in the format itself ( {when:[[HH:mm]]} ) or format the value first and pass the string. Tests Two tests in MarkupTests : MarkupInterpolated_Should_Not_Throw_When_Object_ToString_Contains_Brackets uses the class from the issue and asserts both that nothing throws and that the output is exactly This is a This[contains, braces]. . Checking the exact output matters: an escaping bug can also show up as doubled brackets, not just as a crash. MarkupInterpolated_Should_Preserve_Null_For_Custom_Formatter passes a formatter that prints <null> and checks that it still sees the null . @patriksvensson approved it with a "LGTM 👍". It was my second PR to the project, after the Align measurement fix . References spectreconsole/spectre.console issue #1763 : Interpolation crashes if object contains square brackets. spectreconsole/spectre.console PR #2118 : Fix escaping of interpolated arguments in markup. Spectre.Console 0.56.0 release notes . Spectre.Console docs, Markup . Microsoft Learn, IDE0071: Simplify interpolation .

articles.title: List`1[System.Int32] is not a style: escaping interpolated values in Spectre.Console markup
articles.headline: Spectre.Console fixes interpolated value escaping bug in 0.56.0 release
articles.summary: Spectre.Console 0.56.0 resolves an InvalidOperationException that occurred when interpolated values contained square brackets. The bug affected List, arrays, custom classes, and DateTime with format specifiers. The fix updates EscapeInterpolated to convert non-string arguments via ToString() and escape the result, preserving format specifiers for IFormattable types like dates and numbers. A known limitation remains for format strings that produce brackets, such as {when:[HH:mm]}. The release also includes a test ensuring custom formatters still receive null values correctly.

articles.content: Accessibility work often lives in issue trackers, contribution guidelines, audit reports, team knowledge, and conversations with users. When that information has no predictable home, people who encounter a barrier must search for it, and maintainers lose context as contributors and project ownership change. An ACCESSIBILITY.md file, now visible on repository overview pages, gives a project one durable place to explain its accessibility goals, contributor expectations, supported environments, known limitations, and process for reporting barriers. GitHub makes accessibility statements easier to find GitHub now recognizes the ACCESSIBILITY.md file in the repository’s root, .github/ directory, or docs/ directory. A repository can also inherit a statement from its organization’s .github/ repository. For public repositories, maintainers can add or propose a statement from Insights > Community Standards using a concise starter document. GitHub’s community health files help people understand how a project works: Contribution guidelines explain how to propose changes Codes of conduct establish expectations for participation Security policies explain how to report vulnerabilities Recognizing ACCESSIBILITY.md gives accessibility information a dedicated place alongside that guidance. New repositories also include an accessibility issue label by default. The statement explains how to report a barrier and what to expect next, while the label helps maintainers organize and track the resulting work. Accessibility statements make project practices visible GitHub CLI’s accessibility statement , for example, documents settings, known barriers, and workarounds. It explains why table output can be difficult to follow with a screen reader and provides a command that prints pull request numbers and titles one per line instead. It also asks contributors changing prompts or output to show the results with relevant accessibility settings enabled. Developers using the CLI get a specific workaround; developers contributing to it get clear expectations for their changes. The GitHub Annotation Toolkit’s accessibility statement documents a limitation of its Figma library: annotations use canvas position, connecting lines, and matching numbers to visually convey relationships. Access to individual canvas objects does not necessarily communicate what those relationships are. The statement gives collaborators a concrete alternative: provide a structured text description that identifies each annotated element, its intended semantics and behavior, and any relevant ordering. For developers preparing or receiving a design handoff, this explains what information needs to accompany the visual annotations. The file also explains how to report accessibility barriers and explicitly states that the library has not undergone keyboard-only or screen-reader testing. Readers get both practical guidance and clear limits on what the project has verified. Showing this information in the repository overview makes it easier to find alongside the project’s other documentation. Document what the project can maintain There is no one fixed format for an ACCESSIBILITY.md file. A small library, command-line tool, documentation site, and large web application have different users, risks, and maintenance capacity. Start with accurate information that the project can keep current. Priorities and goals: Explain why accessibility matters to the project and which user experiences receive attention. Contributor expectations: Describe the accessibility checks, evidence, or review practices expected for changes, including instructions for human contributors and coding agents. Reporting accessibility barriers: Provide a direct, accessible reporting path. Do not require disability disclosure, screenshots, or recordings. Response process: Explain how maintainers acknowledge, triage, track, and communicate about accessibility issues. If the project uses severity levels, let maintainers assign or confirm them during triage. Supported environments: List the platforms, browsers, input methods, and assistive technologies the project supports or has tested. Known limitations: Describe barriers in terms of the affected experience, include available workarounds, and link to tracked remediation work. Ownership and maintenance: Name the team, role, or maintainer responsible for keeping the statement and related practices current. Feedback and improvements: Explain how users and contributors can suggest changes to the statement or the project’s accessibility practices. Keep in mind that a project can name a Web Content Accessibility Guidelines version and level as a target. A target does not establish verified conformance. A conformance claim requires an evaluation and should identify the evaluated scope, date, method, and evaluator. What the most useful ACCESSIBILITY.md files contain The most useful accessibility statements serve people who arrive after something has already gone wrong. Plain language, descriptive links, and a clear reporting route matter more than legal or standards-heavy language. Useful reporting guidance invites relevant context, such as the affected task, page, observed behavior, browser, operating system, and assistive technology. It makes screenshots and recordings optional and avoids asking someone to prove a disability. The statement should also set expectations that maintainers can consistently meet. That can include acknowledgement, status updates, available workarounds, expected timelines, and an opportunity for the reporter to verify a fix. Start with an example and adapt it The Open Source Accessibility Toolkit provides a detailed public example. GitHub’s Community Standards workflow provides a shorter starter with prompts that projects can replace with their own information. The goal is not to produce a perfect policy before publishing the file. Start with accurate information, name the gaps, and update the statement as the project’s accessibility practices mature. Adding an accessibility statement makes accessibility work more discoverable to users, contributors, and maintainers. Normalizing that practice across open source projects helps make accessibility part of how communities plan, build, report, and improve their work. Add an accessibility statement to your repository >

articles.content: The most expensive line in an agent-generated pull request is rarely the wrong one. It is the one you cannot take back. A wrong function body costs you a revert. A dropped column costs you a restore window, a status page, and a postmortem. That asymmetry should drive the review order, not the diff order. This post describes a review pass you run before reading logic: classify every changed path by rollback cost, then decide what to split, what to test, and what to reject outright. The artifact is a git-only classifier plus a decision table. No model required for the classification step, which is the point. The review question that survives a bad diff Most review advice optimizes for spotting wrong logic. That is the part agents are usually good at — they produce plausible, readable code that passes a skim. The failures that actually hurt are structural. A migration that drops a column. A renamed module that breaks an import two services away. A lockfile bump nobody read. A test marked skip to make CI green. Every one of those survives a logic read and fails in production. So flip the order: Classify each changed path by rollback cost . Split anything irreversible into its own PR. Test the rollback, not just the feature. Only then read the logic. Classify before you read The four buckets Irreversible — the change cannot be undone by git revert . Schema migrations, DROP / TRUNCATE , renames that break consumers, deletions of files still referenced elsewhere, published artifacts, secret rotations. Mutating — revertable in git, but the revert is not a no-op. Lockfiles, dependency pins, Dockerfiles, CI workflows, build config, .env shape. Ordinary — application code with normal blast radius. Standard review applies. Additive — new tests, new docs, new files nothing imports yet. Safe to merge ahead of the code that uses them. A PR that mixes buckets is not one PR. That sentence alone resolves a large share of agent PR review disputes, because agents will happily bundle a refactor with a migration if nobody stops them. The classifier The script below is a git-only classifier. As written here it has only been exercised against synthetic repositories — treat it as a starting point you validate, not a tool with a track record. #!/usr/bin/env python3 """ irreversibility_audit.py — rank PR hunks by rollback cost. Usage: python irreversibility_audit.py --base origin/main Requires: git, Python 3.9+. No network access. Exit code 1 if any IRREVERSIBLE path is present. """ import argparse , re , subprocess , sys BUCKETS = [ ( " IRREVERSIBLE " , [ r " (^|/)migrations?/ " , r " (^|/)alembic/versions/ " , r " \.sql$ " , r " (^|/)schema\.prisma$ " ]), ( " MUTATING " , [ r " (^|/)(Dockerfile|docker-compose\.ya?ml)$ " , r " (^|/)\.github/workflows/ " , r " (^|/)(package-lock\.json|poetry\.lock|uv\.lock|go\.sum)$ " , r " (^|/)(pyproject\.toml|package\.json|go\.mod)$ " ]), ( " ADDITIVE " , [ r " (^|/)tests?/ " , r " (^|/)docs?/ " , r " \.md$ " ]), ] RISKY = [ ( " drop-or-truncate " , r " \b(DROP\s+(TABLE|COLUMN)|TRUNCATE)\b " ), ( " not-null-no-default " , r " NOT\s+NULL(?![^\n]*DEFAULT) " ), ( " skip-or-xfail " , r " (@pytest\.mark\.(skip|xfail)|\.skip\(|xit\() " ), ( " swallowed-error " , r " except\s*:\s*$|except\s+Exception\s*:\s*pass " ), ( " destructive-shell " , r " (rm\s+-rf|--force\b|shutil\.rmtree) " ), ( " permissive-mode " , r " chmod\s+0?777|mode=0o?777 " ), ] ORDER = { " IRREVERSIBLE " : 0 , " MUTATING " : 1 , " ORDINARY " : 2 , " ADDITIVE " : 3 } def git ( * args ): return subprocess . run (( " git " ,) + args , capture_output = True , text = True , check = True ). stdout def bucket_for ( path ): for name , pats in BUCKETS : if any ( re . search ( p , path ) for p in pats ): return name return " ORDINARY " def main (): ap = argparse . ArgumentParser () ap . add_argument ( " --base " , default = " origin/main " ) base = ap . parse_args (). base rows = [] for line in git ( " diff " , " --name-status " , f " { base } ...HEAD " ). splitlines (): status , * paths = line . split ( " \t " ) path = paths [ - 1 ] # renames list old + new; audit the destination findings = set () if set ( status ) & { " D " , " R " }: findings . add ( " removes-or-renames-path " ) diff = git ( " diff " , " -U0 " , f " { base } ...HEAD " , " -- " , path ) added = [ l for l in diff . splitlines () if l . startswith ( " + " ) and not l . startswith ( " +++ " )] for label , pat in RISKY : if any ( re . search ( pat , l ) for l in added ): findings . add ( label ) rows . append (( bucket_for ( path ), status , path , sorted ( findings ))) for bucket , status , path , findings in sorted ( rows , key = lambda r : ORDER [ r [ 0 ]]): tail = f " <- { ' , ' . join ( findings ) } " if findings else "" print ( f " { bucket : < 13 } { status : < 4 } { path }{ tail } " ) if any ( r [ 0 ] == " IRREVERSIBLE " for r in rows ): print ( " \n VERDICT: split before merge — irreversible paths present. " ) return 1 return 0 if __name__ == " __main__ " : sys . exit ( main ()) Two honest caveats about the code.
