articles.content: Listen and watch now on YouTube , Apple , and Spotify . See the episode transcript at the top of this page, and timestamps for the episode at the bottom. Brought to You by • turbopuffer – The tpuf eng team is completely redesigning their storage architecture from first principles. And they’re documenting all of it! They made epic progress; take a look: turbopuffer.com/v3 • Antithesis – use AI agents to work on critical systems without worrying about correctness. Antithesis runs your complete system in a hostile environment, analyzes its behavior, and reproduces every issue perfectly. Learn more • Entire – Entire launched its own Git forge, shipped Continuous Memory , and reinvented the pull request (called Trails ). Trails are a much more natural workflow when agents keep pushing new changes, after iterating on feedback – and you have more context and control on when a change is ready to merge. Check it out In this episode What is involved in scaling up large, popular products at places like Slack and GitHub? We get an insider’s view on this from Maude Lemaire , a principal engineer and author of ‘ Refactoring at Scale: Regaining Control of Your Codebase .’ She spent nearly eight years at Slack, where she led the backend performance infrastructure team, before joining GitHub to tackle database scaling challenges. Most recently, she worked on improving performance at Cursor – including time to first token. In this episode of The Pragmatic Engineer , Maude and I dig into the challenges of scaling some of the world’s largest software products. We explore how Slack handled growing numbers of enterprise customers, how it evolved its approach to load testing, and the lessons Maude learned during nearly eight years of scaling Slack’s infrastructure. She also tells us what it was like joining GitHub in 2024 when Copilot was taking off, the challenges of working with GitHub’s gigantic Rails monolith, and how Maude uses AI in her work – while keeping judgment calls and decision-making firmly in her own hands. Takeaways from the conversation with Maude Here are eight interesting points from our discussion: 1. Performance should matter even if there’s no competition. In 2015, the homepage of Rent the Runway took up to 10 seconds to fully load due to a high-resolution hero image on the site. Maude was told it wasn’t an issue because there were no competitors to worry about. She thought differently: “The best competition is competition with yourself, knowing that you can do better, knowing that you can drive a better experience, ” she said. Maude spent some free time on speeding up the website without asking for permission to do so because it was the right call. 2. Slack limits custom emojis to 23 to avoid thundering herds. Here’s an example of a thundering herd : the CEO of a 100,000-member Slack channel posts “everyone gets Friday off!” In response, people start posting custom emojis – hundreds of them. The problem is that every single custom emoji has to fan out to all 100,000 users. With 10 custom emojis, that’s 1,000,000 fan-outs, with 100 it’s 10,000,000; a lot of network load! Slack limits custom emojis to 23 to avoid this problem. In reality, the absent 24th custom emoji is not missed. 3. Event floods can cripple the machines of Slack’s power users. Event floods are the cousin of thundering herds: they occur when a single client is overwhelmed by events coming through its own WebSocket. For example, when an IT worker is logged into lots of busy channels and they all receive the “everyone gets Friday off!” message – along with all the associated custom emojis and messages. This “power user” gets a sudden influx of messages with no deduplication and they struggle. 4. Load testing 500,000 WebSocket connections the simple way would have cost $150,000 per run. A new customer with 500,000 users was about to sign up to Slack, and Maude needed to run a load test to confirm the service could handle the load. Initially, she planned to spin up headless Chrome instances – each instance running a Slack session, and that would have cost $0.37 per five-hour session, per instance. The total price would’ve been crazily expensive. Instead, Maude built a tool called Koi Pond that spins up slimmed-down versions of Slack (‘Koi’), written in Go to establish the WebSocket connections. 5. Active Record downside: too much database load! GitHub used to be a Ruby on Rails monolith, which used Active Record as a database abstraction layer. This caused unexpected load: GitHub’s home page fetched live data from the database for most reloads, and loading the home page regularly triggered 100 SQL queries across three database clusters. This revealed a downside of abstractions like Active Record to Maude: when devs used it, they didn’t know or care about the additional load they unwittingly placed on the database while fetching data for whatever they were working on. 6. GitHub could not add more than 16 database shards because of scatter query problems. A scatter query is one without a primary key (a sharding key), and it needs to be run across all shard instances . But more shards make such queries slower. Back in the day at GitHub, lots of queries made through Active Record (many on the homepage) were scatter queries. This limitation prevented GitHub from adding more than 16 shards. I find this detail fascinating: it shows why a developer-friendly abstraction (Active Record) can actually cause severe pain at the infra level! 7. For platform work, Maude personally verifies everything she gets from an LLM. When doing foundational work, Maude pays close attention to verifying the output of LLMs because she believes that ambitious structures can only be built on stable foundations. It’s an interesting approach to separate “foundational” and “non-foundational” work in order to give more attention to the former, most critical, type. 8. Platform and product engineers should rotate more.

articles.title: Scaling Slack and GitHub with Maude Lemaire
articles.headline: Slack limits custom emojis to 23 to avoid thundering herds
articles.summary: Maude Lemaire, principal engineer and author of 'Refactoring at Scale,' discusses infrastructure challenges at Slack and GitHub. Key points include Slack limiting custom emojis to 23 to prevent network overload from 'thundering herds,' building Koi Pond to test 500,000 WebSocket connections affordably, and GitHub's Active Record causing excessive database load with 100 SQL queries per homepage reload. The conversation also covers GitHub's 16-shard limit due to scatter query problems and LLM verification practices for platform work.

articles.content: Listen to this post: Good morning, This week’s Stratechery Interview is with Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi . Goodarzi took a very non-traditional path to Silicon Valley, joining Intuit in 2004 after working at Siemens and Honeywell. After managing business units across the company he became CEO in 2019, and is taking on the challenge of figuring out how one of tech’s oldest software companies manages the AI paradigm shift. In this interview we discuss Goodarzi’s background and the what it takes to be an effective generalist, and get his take on how Intuit has thrived for 44 years. We discuss the shift from Quicken to Quickbooks, the TurboTax business, and how Goodarzi thinks about the consumer space today. Then we talk about accountants, Intuit’s most important customer acquisition channel, and how the company wants to change the profession from partners to customers via AI. I present the case to Goodarzi that Intuit seems like its being disrupted, and he makes the case why they are well positioned to actual grow their market. We also touch on acquisitions like Credit Karma and Mailchimp, and how Intuit has managed business model changes in the past, and what needs to change in the future. As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player. On to the Interview: An Interview With Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi About Accounting and AI This interview is lightly edited for clarity. Topics: Being a Generalist | Intuit History | TurboTax and Credit Karma | The Future of Accountants | Disruption | Mailchimp | Intuit’s AI Future Being a Generalist Sasan Goodarzi, welcome to Stratechery. Sasan Goodarzi: Thank you for having me, I’m a big fan of all the work that you do. It’s great to be a part of it. Well, we’ll get to my relationship with Intuit, which I’ve had for many years. Big fan? I’m going to have to think about that one. We are here to talk about Intuit, a company that you have been at, with a brief break, for over 20 years. Before we get to that, however, tell me about your background, which is a very interesting one. Let’s start with where you were born. SG: Yes, I was born in Tehran, in Iran, and I am the youngest of three — 13 years younger than the other two brothers. I was told I was special, I think I was an accident, so there you go. And back then, you’d ship your kids to the U.S. because everybody wanted to come to the U.S. to study and so my brothers were in the U.S. already studying, and my parents decided to do an experiment with me and shipped me to the U.S. at the age of nine and I was very fortunate, because the revolution actually happened. Got it. So you had already left before then, I wasn’t quite sure on that timing. SG: Yeah, yeah. I was very fortunate, I left before the revolution, about eight to nine months before the revolution, and have been in the U.S. ever since. Where did you end up in the U.S.? SG: I came to Orlando, Florida of all places, because my brothers were going to the University of Central Florida. And, by the way, back then we used to say, “U Can’t Finish”, that’s what we called it, but it’s a great university. But anyways, for that reason, I was in Orlando until my early 20s, until I started being moved by Honeywell. Every couple of years, I was going to a different state, which was a lot of fun, and eventually ended up in California. You studied electrical engineering, right? And then you were at Honeywell and Invensys. What were you doing there? I mean, it doesn’t seem quite the obvious path to being CEO of Intuit, to say the least. SG: Not at all. In fact, it’s advice I give, career advice I give to folks. I actually started at Siemens, I was a technical marketing person, which really — I don’t know why they called it marketing, it was all a technical role that supported our field sales folks. I was in the power generation business unit at Siemens so I used to go pitch why our power generation was better than anybody else’s. I don’t think they need much marketing these days in the Siemens Power Generation Unit. SG: (laughing) Yeah that’s right, they don’t. I did that for four years and frankly, I didn’t know what I wanted to do with my life, because in the meantime, I was doing startups on the side. In fact, before I even started at Siemens, I did a startup called Lazer Cables — with, at that time, a very good friend that was actually the genius behind the idea of fiber optics for the music industry, so I was dabbling in a lot of different stuff. When I was at Siemens, I love the company, but I was wondering, “Is the corporate world cut out for me?”, and I got recruited to Honeywell. And at Honeywell, they put me — it was like business development. In essence, they put me in charge of something they were experimenting with, which was just down my alley, because it was, in essence, a startup as part of Honeywell and I fell in love with the company because of that. I was there, I think like eight years. So is this — was this going to different states? Was that because Honeywell, being a defense contractor, they just have to source from everywhere? Is that the connection? SG: Yeah, but I was in the industrial home automation division.

articles.content: Before we start: I’m in San Francisco this week and there are a few remaining spots for these live events (registration required): Wednesday (4 Nov): The Pragmatic Engineer Unplugged at the iconic SFJAZZ Center. With Diogo Almeida (creator of Jev & co-inventor of ChatGPT), and Bryan Cantrill (cofounder and CTO of Oxide). Thursday (5 Nov): System Update at The Howard SF. With Karri Saarinen (Linear), Kath Korevec (OpenAI), David Cramer (Sentry) and Adam Rogal (DoorDash) Also, this week there will be no issue of The Pulse on Thursday. Regular scheduling returns next week! In September, when The Pragmatic Engineer turned five , I announced an essay challenge, inviting readers to write about how things have changed in tech workplaces and in our projects, for the chance to win a grand prize of $10,000 awarded to our favorite article. We received 125 submissions, covering a wide range of viewpoints and experiences. Many thanks to everyone who took part. In today’s issue, we publish the winning piece in full. Congratulations to software engineer Neil Kakkar ! We appreciate the sheer volume of data that Neil has collected about how his own output has changed over time. Neil is a dev based in London, with nine years of professional experience; he has interned at Google, and been a software engineer at Bloomberg, Posthog, and Tano. His previous workplace, PostHog, is an open source project, which must’ve been useful for gathering historic data. In a follow-up issue, we’ll highlight runner-up essays, and link to the ones that impressed us for the effort on show and interesting thoughts. With that, it’s over to Neil. He covers: Two eras of shipping . Until last year, he was merging between eight and 20 pull requests (PRs) per month. But since joining an AI-native startup, Neil now ships 200+ PRs per month, approximately a tenfold increase. Old constraints that disappeared. No more communications overhead or code reviews. The tradeoff: moving faster and breaking things. New constraints that appeared. Too much context switching (thrashing), losing shared context, pacing yourself is harder, less focus on design, and worries about AI plan limits. How AI is changing software engineering. Everyone needs to be onboard with AI to get the benefits at work, encouraging experimentation makes a difference, and many existing technologies and processes crack under the change. I’ve been working at an AI native startup for the past eight months. Before joining Tano , I was at PostHog for four years, a fast moving pre-AI startup, and started my career at Bloomberg , a big fintech private company, where I spent three years. All three workplaces are different: Bloomberg is huge, with 20,000 people and very defined processes. PostHog is smaller, at around 10 people when I joined, and now at 200. At Tano, I was the first engineer and we’re now around 10 people in total. In each job, I’ve seen what a difference speed and culture make, and more recently, how culture needs to change to keep up with AI. To back things up, I use in-depth stats about my work at PostHog and Tano. I also have some very rough numbers from Bloomberg. By far, I’ve written more code and made a lot more PRs at Tano than I did at PostHog, and a major part of this is down to AI. Facilitating the shift is engineering culture. One disclaimer before we get into it: the PostHog stats are from pre-AI. I’ve been following their journey, and PostHog is as “AI-pilled” as it gets now, and output is increasing significantly. In this article, I treat it as a ‘pre-AI baseline’ for excellent engineering work. Tano is a fast-moving AI-native startup, founded after AI agents emerged. 1. Two eras of shipping Let’s start with some raw numbers. I’m shipping 11x more PRs at Tano than at PostHog, where I shipped 2.4x as many as I did at Bloomberg. At Bloomberg, I was just starting my career, so I wasn’t the fastest, and moving to PostHog opened my eyes to what a fast-moving startup culture really looks like: we were encouraged to take responsibility, ship things quickly, listen to customers, and solve their issues ASAP. At Bloomberg and PostHog there was a high bar for code: everything had to be peer reviewed, and as I became senior, I spent a big chunk of my time reviewing code. PRs can be an easily gamed metric, but I was not trying to game the numbers, so they’re an honest representation of the work done. Below are details of everything I worked on to justify the 11x PR multiplier. What I worked on I joined PostHog as a full stack software engineer and worked across the product, from the ingestion pipeline to optimising our analytics queries for funnels and retention on Clickhouse, scaling it up to handle a billion+ events scale, and eventually building out the experimentation product from scratch. I later led the Feature Success team, where we built out two new products: surveys and early access features, while improving experimentation and feature flags. I joined Tano as a founding engineer and focused on a similar breadth of product as at PostHog, but all compressed into eight months instead of 45. I built out our new affiliate platform, made our content monitoring system a lot more efficient, and did some big migrations, like moving the entire agent architecture to a new system with persistent memory, better tools, and superior observability. Here’s a summary of work I did at both companies: How I work today At PostHog until late 2024, the extent of AI was tab completion. It was great for automating menial work like repetitive test cases, but was a long way away from today’s autonomous agents that can build an entire feature with no human input. When I joined Tano this year, Claude Code Desktop was already present with really good agent support, and could build out entire features with little hand-holding.

articles.content: Listen to this post : Log in to listen From Bloomberg this morning at 2 a.m. Central: Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress in a midterm election landslide that amounted to a rejection of President Donald Trump following widespread voter discontent with the economy and the war in Iran. Across the country, Democrats scored victories in GOP strongholds, flipping at least seven Senate seats and winning House races in districts Republicans easily carried in 2024. Several news organizations projected that Democrats would win the House, while Decision Desk HQ projected they took the Senate. I have no doubt that Iran and the economy played significant roles in this election; what stood out to me, however, was very much Stratechery fodder. Specifically, I watch a lot of sports, and particularly this fall, watched a lot of baseball. My Milwaukee Brewers — excuse me, my World Champion Milwaukee Brewers — demanded my full attention, which also meant I saw a lot of campaign ads, and by far the most common topic, at least here in Wisconsin, was data centers. Moreover, it was never entirely clear which way it cut politically: both parties were anti-data center, accusing their opponent of being the opposite. Meanwhile in Texas, from Yahoo Finance : A strong showing by Democrats in Texas swept Gina Hinojosa into office as the state’s first Democratic governor since 1990 in a contest closely watched by Big Tech companies. The state is considered a bellwether for government restrictions on AI data centers…Hinojosa, Texas’ first Latina governor, has pledged to impose a moratorium on data center construction in Texas, which accounts for more than 25% of planned US capacity by 2030. Republican incumbent Greg Abbott, I would note, already declared a moratorium on new data-center permits in September; that’s how much of a hot-button issue this is, including in the state that is the biggest opportunity and beneficiary of the data center buildout. So yeah, this is a Stratechery topic of concern. The Data Center Veto Earlier this year, while writing about data center opposition , I said: There really wasn’t widespread opposition to data centers when they were being built for the Internet generally; indeed, local governments would compete for them, eager for the economic benefits that came during their construction and the long-term tax benefits once they were operational. In other words, it seems pretty clear that the current wave of opposition can’t be divorced from AI — you know, the technology that in the best case scenario is going to take everyone’s jobs, and in the worst case scenario end the human race. I do not, I don’t think, need to explain to you why this is not a very compelling message, and, in the very long run, I do think that humans will have economic value . At the same time, it’s hard to explain the huge amount of investment that is going into AI, not just at the model level but also in terms of data centers, without admitting that a big part of the thesis is that AI can not just increase the top line for companies, but also increase the bottom line — i.e. replace the jobs of some number of humans. Again, I’m generally an optimist here, but this already happened with the first wave of IT . That leads to an interesting contrast to globalization: when companies were closing down American factories and laying off workers and moving operations to China, none of the affected towns or workers had a say. They just suddenly no longer had a job, and a huge number of cities across the Rust Belt no longer had a reason to exist. People simply had to move, or worse, retreat to things like alcohol or drugs. AI, however, is the opposite: building data centers requires permission, which is to say that people actually have a say. Again, I am not at all saying that these people are well informed about data centers, or about the economic impact on their communities, much less the economic impact of AI generally; what I am noting is that people who didn’t have a say in globalization are suddenly finding they do have a say about AI, and it’s not a surprise they are expressing their disapproval by blocking data centers. That message was loud and clear last spring; now it is deafening, and it’s tempting to say that tech, particularly the frontier labs, have no one to blame but themselves. In fact, however, some of the biggest culprits may, in the long run, be some of the biggest beneficiaries of the anti-data center wave. My thesis — driven not just by national results and the Texas governorship, but also the fact that, as this thread documents , nearly every relevant local ballot measure opposing data centers won or is winning ( the only exception so far was in North Dakota ) — is that the constraint on AI dispersion has shifted once again. First we were short on compute, but that ramped; now we are short on memory, but that will ramp; we were coming close to being short on power, but that will be rectified. The final constraint is political, and that may be the most imposing constraint of all. Not only is it harder to solve, but it actually interferes with solving the other constraints. Many of the theories about AI assume that it becomes a commodity; I think it’s just as likely we are looking at scarcity for much longer than we expected, which will have ripple effects on everything. Ten Takes To that end, here — with the caveat that nothing leads to hot takes you regret like an election — are ten perspectives on what a permanently impaired ability to build might mean.

articles.content: Release: datasette-apps 0.3a0 Datasette Apps adds support for hosting and editing custom HTML applications inside of Datasette. These can be created by hand, but it's easier to create them using LLMs via Datasette Agent . This release improves that integration: Apps can now be tagged in Datasette Agent chat messages by typing # , which autocompletes from the apps the user has permission to view. New app_add_stored_queries() and app_remove_stored_queries() tools let the agent manage which stored queries an app is allowed to call. Granting a write query requires approval from the user first. app_create() now checks that each requested stored query exists and that the user can view it, and asks the user to approve any write queries before the app is created. The "View app" buttons shown by the agent tools, and the links on # app references, now open the app full screen in the Datasette Agent panel.

articles.content: Sometimes when I read a post, I get the growing feeling that I'm reading the output of an LLM. I can't necessarily define why, although there are the common tells (it's not the em-dashes, it's the load-bearing tapestries). As I do this my desire to read on atrophies, sometimes to the point of revulsion There are tools out there that claim to be able to tell the difference between LLM-written prose and the old-fashioned biological product. I'm wary of them, partly due skeptism about their accuracy, but also because it rather misses the point. The reaction to LLM-Voice is a human one, that sense that we are in an uncanny valley of prose. By the time I'd reach for a tool to tell me what I'm reading, it's already too late, even if it confidently tells me there's no LLM present. I'm also suspicious of my own ability to accurately recognize LLM voice. Language changes over time, so a common sign of age is complaining about the language of the youngs. I'm inclined to bristle at prose that talks about “adopting a new sales motion ,” or “a sharp round-up of news”. But I've heard these constructs coming out of human mouths, so that's more a generational difference rather than between carbon and silicon. (And as a transplanted Brit, don't get me started on Americanisms, I'm sure I'll get used to them momentarily.) Right now I urge authors to be extra-wary of LLM-Voice. In particular I strongly recommend that authors should not fall into the trap of getting the LLM to write a draft. Even if it's edited by a human, it's very hard to expel the LLM-Voice - thus causing the uncanny valley reaction. 1 Even accepting suggestions of rephrasing is dangerous. I have heard of people using LLMs to develop outline and structure, that may be ok, but only as far as an outline. 2 Authors should fill the prose themselves. Say Your Writing is even more important in the age of LLMs. I habitually speak the words in my head and then write them down (and then edit what I've just written). This advice is particularly important to anyone who has any desire to communicate regularly with writing. Like many things, learning to be a good writer relies on lots of practice. It's a skill worth the time to acquire, but surrendering to an LLM will undermine any progress. In time it may be that LLMs will be so good that we can't tell the difference. In many ways, that's more worrying. Like most writers, I find writing an almost-essential tool for thinking. Often it's only by writing something down, that I can really get my thoughts on a topic into coherence. I've often started an essay knowing I don't really understand something, but the act of wrestling with the words forces me to overcome my confusions. As more people delegate writing to LLMs they will also delegate thinking and comprehension to LLMs. I don't want to do that, where's the fun of writing then? Although avoiding LLM-Voice is a general rule, it isn't an absolute one. An important example is that of Jim Highsmith (who contributes to this site). He finds working with an LLM is essential to his writing to overcome the bane of Parkinson's disease . I'll gladly deal with LLM-Voice in order to continue imbibing my old friend's wisdom. A more awkward case is that of translation. Many of my colleagues aren't comfortable in English, it is their second or fourth language. Some have found LLM translation an important part to their communication with those of us who know rather less Marathi. But I also would prefer rather a genuine human's clunky prose to the smooth but soulless LLM. There are situations where it would be reasonable for even a native Englishman to let LLMs write the prose. Such as if I'm writing a form letter to an official, or preparing a report I suspect no-one will ever read 3 . Maybe most documentation in the future will only be read by LLMs, and they won't have my uncanny valley worries. But if I want to communicate with humans, my humanity has to shine (or at least ooze) out of my prose. Notes 1: Very hard, but not impossible. I've come across one case where I do know the first draft was entirely done by LLM, but I detected no LLM Voice when I read the final piece. It did, however, need a professional editor at a major periodical publication to clean it up. 2: My policy on this site, is that anyone who uses AI to help them write should declare how they used it, usually in the acknowledgments. This is partly for transparency, and partly so that readers can learn useful ways to use AI. In my own case, I don't use AI for generating prose, nor for help in structure. The only way I use it for writing is as a search tool (but I verify any information by going to the source). 3: Michael Nygard commented: “There you really aren't trying to communicate thoughts from one person to other people. You're communicating with a process rather than a human. A human may open the envelope but that person is acting as a component in a cybernetic organism.” Acknowledgements Alessio Ferri, Caer Sanders, Ian Cartwright, Jie Jessie Xia, Joshua Kerievsky, Michael Feathers, Michael Nygard, Scott Davies, and Wei Zhang commented on drafts of this post. I did not use AI or LLMs in any way while writing this post.

articles.headline: Fowler warns against LLM prose causing uncanny valley reaction
articles.summary: Martin Fowler warns that LLM-generated prose triggers an uncanny valley reaction, making readers uncomfortable. articles.content: TL;DR Good developers’ caution about agentic development comes from knowing that built isn’t the same as working in production. I’ve been surprised by how many excellent developers have been hesitant to go all in on coding agents. These are people who usually try new ways of working before anyone else and in many cases invent new tools and practices that support building the application well. So why have we had so much reluctance? The easy (lazy?) answer is that they love writing code, or they’re worried about their jobs. I’m sure that’s true for some people, some of the time. And I know it is true for some of the developers I talk to but I always felt there was something else, another fear hiding behind those obvious ones. When we put together the Technology Radar every six months I try to block out a chunk of time for us to do an open space. In September, a discussion we had on agentic development, which pushed it to its limits, finally helped me see clearly what that fear is. Building it right Thoughtworkers care deeply about building the right thing and building it right . It’s pretty much our default way of working and thinking and it’s where many of the practices and technologies we invented and championed came from. We want software that is useful and helpful, can be changed next year, and doesn’t fall over in production. Our developers adopted, championed or invented some of the first versions of continuous integration, pairing, automated testing, continuous delivery, microservices and many others early because they helped us build the software right. Early coding agents made it very easy to produce code, including code we wouldn’t have wanted anywhere near production, written by people who have not learned about the chasm between building something and making it run in production safely. The tools have improved enormously, but experienced developers still have questions. Are we confident this is the right behaviour? Does it work as expected? Are these the right boundaries? Will we be able to evolve it? Does it abide by the principles and practices we learned the hard way to give us confidence it will meet the needs of the customer and stay up in production? What happens when something fails? Will another team be able to live with it? And so on. Underneath all of those sits a bigger question. How much can we trust a system when nobody has experience of building it this way? Let me state that another way. Nearly every system we have in production now was built the old way, by hand, by people we could trust (hopefully). Everything we build now is the new way and we have not lived with that yet. After more than 25 years in technology, I’ve come to value the judgment people develop through experience. I regularly put similar questions to models and to senior technologists at Thoughtworks. For the difficult questions, I still get more useful answers from the humans or maybe more insightful with very specific experience that helps me better understand the point. They challenge the premise, recognise a pattern from something that went wrong ten years ago, or spot the organisational problem hiding inside the technical one. I can now access an extraordinary amount of information. I still need people who can help me think through what matters, I still need wisdom and insight. That type judgment is exactly what hesitant experienced developers are trying to protect. And I want to be clear: they are not hesitant to use a coding assistant, they are hesitant to go all in and let the agents do all the execution. They are hesitant to take their hand off the wheel because they don’t have full confidence the agents have the right guardrails in place to run off on their own. A week at the whiteboard Recently, Giles Alexander, our Regional CTO for Europe, brought senior engineers, infrastructure consultants and product people together for a week of working in exactly this way. No code written by anyone. Everything built by agents. The point wasn’t to prove that an airline application could be built in a week. (Funnily enough they got 80% done and we all know what that means… you can’t make stuff up!) The purpose of the experiment was to learn what happens to the team’s work when agents do all of the coding. You can read some of what they learned here . What struck me in our conversations was how much time they spent at the whiteboard. Working out the domain. Drawing boundaries. Deciding what should happen next and making plans the agents could act on. Meanwhile, the agents kept producing code beyond the team’s working day. The humans were also designing the feedback around that work: tests, contracts, architecture checks and a delivery pipeline. They were working out how to give agents enough freedom to make progress while keeping confidence in the result. Most of the work at the keyboard was directing agents to put this learning into the harness, so the building and testing agents got it right on the next run and they could have more confidence in what they built. Interestingly in the end the product person committed more feature code than anyone else on the team. When I asked them to estimate they said they spend about ⅔ of their time at the whiteboard and ⅓ on the harness, which could give us some clue as to how developers will work in the future, but before you get ahead of yourself redesigning your team, that’s not the end of the story… The application ran. The build was red. The application ran, but the build was frequently red. It worked on their machine - again you couldn’t make this up if you tried! A constant red build gives me the ick. A red build should mean something: stop, investigate, fix it.

articles.title: Why are good developers so wary of agentic development?
articles.headline: Experienced developers wary of agentic development due to production readiness concerns
articles.summary: Thoughtworks CTO Rachel Laycock explains why senior developers hesitate to fully adopt agentic development. Despite rapid code generation, teams worry about trust, boundaries, and the gap between building and running software safely. An experiment building an airline application entirely with agents revealed that humans spent significant time at whiteboards defining domains and designing feedback mechanisms like tests and pipelines. The application frequently had red builds, raising concerns about CI/CD reliability and the ability to spot real failures. The experiment highlights the need for new practices to manage batch sizes and ensure stability as AI adoption increases.

articles.content: Andrej Karpathy sees a widening gap in how people see LLM capabilities. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time. Many of my colleagues are living in a world where LLM capabilities are stunning, but it’s easy to forget that’s not what most people experience. One thing I do is use free-tier LLM chatbots, and I’m still finding that while most of the time they are useful, their unreliability undermines much of that usefulness. Yes, you can argue that I’m not using frontier tools or a forceful enough harness, but that’s true of most regular folks too. To understand their perception, it’s handy to experience it. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ That observation particularly resonates with me today, as I’ve just spent the weekend at Foocamp, an open space event run by O’Reilly. It was full of those who are experiencing that vertigo of LLM capabilities, so it felt very much like being in a bubble of those on the bleeding edge. While it’s worth remembering that that’s not a typical view of what’s happening, it’s good to see what those explorers are experiencing. (As I talk about this, I’m applying the Chatham House rule , if anyone wants attribution, let me know.) A couple of folks talked about doing immersion courses to help teach developers how to do agentic engineering . The idea is to get people out of their usual work environment, and spend one or two weeks with experienced coaches, learning how to use these tools well. Such things remind me very much of the Extreme Programming immersion classes I was involved with at the turn of the century. As with that, the experience of building something is important to understand such a new style of work. Unsurprisingly the coaches observed that the biggest impact wasn’t technical, but emotional. New tools are just new tools, but these tools change basic assumptions of what it means to be a software developer, which for many people challenges their identity. One coach said how his main job was to take such people out for a walk to a coffee shop, so they could process what’s happening. (This reminds me of a participant of the Extreme Programming immersion who was so horrified by the use of a non-locking version-control system (CVS) that he walked out of the class on the first day.) ❄ ❄ I’m wary of talking about themes to an event where I attend less than one-tenth of the sessions, but a topic I kept coming across was how large enterprises were embracing this technology - or rather not. One participant used a lovely metaphor: corporations have acquired a Swiss-army knife, but are only using the toothpick. I see plenty of decent reasons for this: it’s one thing for a startup or individual to use a hot technology, but there’s a big difference between a website going down and your factories grinding to a halt. Big organizations involve workflows involving lots of people that have built up over many years - they don’t change easily. Security concerns abound, the lethal trifecta still lurks. In particular good use of AI in enterprises relies on good data, and many such organizations don’t have their data in a decent shape. The path to getting agent-ready data isn’t trivial and it’s hard to see how we can get the knife and saw out until enterprises are much further down that path. One thing that struck me is that there was little conversation about this at Foocamp - a sign of its visibility among the people there. ❄ ❄ I very much enjoyed Foocamp, but events like this are always a mix of excitement and dread. I knew very few of the people there, so it was a great opportunity to get out of my own social bubble. But I also find it nearly impossible to walk up to people I don’t know (or know slightly) and impose my company on them. The great thing about unconferences is that the nature of the sessions make it plausible for someone like me to engage in conversation during them, and begin some tentative links. Also I thank the many folks there who were friendly to me as I casually walked around trying to hide how much I was panicking. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Laurie Voss says today is 1997 On Saturday, Apollo’s chief economist Torsten Slok published No Signs of AI Payoff Outside the Tech Sector. It’s short and it’s blunt: outside of 7 major tech companies, there is no data yet to support a productivity gain that justifies all the money pouring into tech. My position is that he’s half right: are valuations too high? Absolutely. We’re in a bubble, and it’s absolutely going to pop. But does that mean investing in AI is a waste of money? Absolutely not, and using this early data to try and decide that question would be like trying to decide in 1997 whether the Internet was going to pay off. The data just isn’t there yet, because these things take time. I’m not as sure as he is that we can peg today to 1997 rather than 1999, but I agree that this boom bears a lot of resemblance to the dotcom boom (although I think this one is bigger). While many dotcom companies crashed (I always think of pets.com and webvan) he’s right to point out that anyone who invested in Amazon in 1997 did very well. Where might those good investments be this time? if you can build something that proves you got the answer, AI can get the answer much faster than you can, and there are real productivity gains to be had doing that generally.

articles.content: Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a "blog post", but it's paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model - literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I've been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I'm delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well! Weight-Space Programming Here's the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights: Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x. All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming . The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models. spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use. I'm going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two. The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games - Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up , it's an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question: The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response. The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs . The exp1_which_game folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games: breakout/prompt.txt freeway/prompt.txt pacman/prompt.txt pong/prompt.txt I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others. Trying it out with Qwen 3.8 27B and other models The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a -f/--fragment option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this: llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/breakout/prompt.txt \ -m openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro This example requires the llm-openrouter plugin installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here's what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro , which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens. But how about Qwen 3.8 27B ? That's still my favorite model to run on my own laptop - it's just 17GB (I use this version ) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025. I fired up LM Studio , ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command: LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900 \ llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/pacman/prompt.txt \ -m lmstudio/qwen/qwen3.8-27b (I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue .) After 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens, Qwen on my laptop returned a response that ended like this (here's the reasoning trace ): Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets. Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards. Confidence: 72% This is impressive. I tried it on two of the other games as well. It identified Pong ( reasoning ) in 1h 4m 54s: Pong — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object. Description: The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized. Confidence: 75% And Breakout ( reasoning ) in 52m 25s: Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game. Description: The agent is a paddle on the bottom row and moves left/right to keep a ball in play; the ball moves around the upper grid, and bricks/reward targets in the top rows give reward when hit, while missing the ball/hitting the bottom wall ends the episode or gives penalty. Confidence: 88% Qwen failed at the Freeway prompt, which didn't surprise me considering that game is more obscure than the other three.

The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a "blog post", but it's paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine…
articles.title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
articles.headline: Qwen 3.8 27B on laptop can interpret and modify model weights
articles.summary: A new paper demonstrates that frontier models can natively read and write neural network weights without tools. Qwen 3.8 27B running on a laptop successfully identified games including Pac-Man and Pong from raw model weights after 46 minutes of reasoning. The model also fixed reasoning loops in Qwen3.5-0.8B by editing 0.016% of weights, improving MATH-500 scores from 7.9% to 48.1%. The research introduces 'Weight-Space Programming,' showing LLMs can analyze model behaviors and make targeted weight changes from scratch.

articles.content: Before we start: I’m in SF this week and next, hosting these free-to-attend events (registration required). If you’re in the area, hopefully I'll see you at one of them: The Pragmatic Engineer Unplugged : Wednesday (4 Nov), 5pm-7:30pm. With Diogo Almeida (creator of Jev & co-inventor of ChatGPT), and Bryan Cantrill (cofounder and CTO of Oxide). We still have space left, RSVP here . System Update : Thursday (5 Nov) 5pm-8pm. We have some last spots left, RSVP here . Listen and watch now on YouTube , Apple , and Spotify . See the episode transcript at the top of this page, and timestamps for the episode at the bottom. Brought to You by • turbopuffer – The tpuf eng team is completely redesigning their storage architecture from first principles. And they’re documenting all of it! They made epic progress, take a look: turbopuffer.com/v3 • Linear – one of the big challenges for us devs is the sheer amount of code to review. Linear Diffs is a new feature to review PRs inside of Linear, with all the context in one place. It also supports stacked PRs. Check it out • WorkOS – WorkOS built Airlock, the authorization layer for AI agents. It evaluates every request against the agent’s intent + your rules and either allows it, denies it, or routes it to a human. Works with Claude Code, Codex & MCP gateways. Give it a spin In this episode An engineer who helped create today’s software engineering curriculum now says to burn down almost all of it. What’s the cause of this contradiction? We find out from the lead author of Software Engineering at Google . Titus Winters spent more than a decade at Google, where he led its readability program and built Abseil , Google’s open-sourced foundational C++ libraries. He is currently a Senior Principal Scientist at Adobe, where he focuses on developer experience and productivity. In this episode of The Pragmatic Engineer podcast , Titus and I discuss how his team tackled a massive refactoring project across Google’s 250-million-line C++ codebase, why Google made testing mandatory, and his work on updating the ACM/IEEE undergraduate computer science curriculum guidelines. We also explore why traditional productivity metrics miss some of AI’s biggest benefits, what needs to change in CS education, and how new engineers can stand out. Takeaways from the conversation with Titus Titus is a deep thinker and has worked on some very interesting projects. Here are 12 things that stick out to me from our chat. 1. Was refactoring 250M+ lines of C++ code the largest refactoring task of all time? This happened at Google in 2010, a few months after Titus joined the search giant. An internal email asked for volunteers to help clean up old C++ code, some of it written by the very first Googlers. A team of a dozen people was assembled. Google had close to 250M lines of code at the time, edited by 10,000 engineers. Titus recalled the cleanup: “We were replacing the foundation of the Empire State Building. We were not allowed to close the building or block traffic. Oh, and we discovered nuclear waste in the basement.” 2. The refactoring was done with advanced language parsing techniques, long before LLMs existed. Back in 2010, there were no LLMs for this giant refactor. Here’s what the team did: Parse : ran a MapReduce over the whole codebase. The mapper parsed every build target into an abstract syntax tree Match : match exact call patterns in the tree Code generation: generated edits to be made by the machine Coexist : make the old API and new API work side-by-side Shard : once the new API is ready to go, split the edits by directory, and send them out in batches Block the old: make sure nobody copied the old pattern back into the code Delete : remove the old API The clang-format toolkit exists because Titus and his team needed it for this refactor. 3. Google made automated tests mandatory after Search could no longer ship regularly. Around 2007, Search, the flagship product, was unable to ship at a monthly cadence any more, and the best they could ship to production was quarterly. Almost every change at Google touched Search’s code, even things like a change to Gmail. To clamp down, Google, as an org, mandated that every change was to be accompanied by a test. Over time, Search returned to its former higher cadence. 4. Google’s readability program might have been the largest educational program ever in tech. To make a code change at Google, two people need to sign off that change through a code review: An “owner” of the file/project: someone on the team with domain knowledge A “readability” reviewer: an engineer certified to be a “readability” expert in the given language that the change was made in Google’s first engineer, Craig Silverstein, walked each new dev hire through their first change. Java teams turned this approach into mentoring, where experienced reviewers were assigned to review all changes in a round-robin fashion. And soon enough, a formalized readability program was built for all languages. When Titus left Google three months ago, 10,000+ engineers were enrolled in readability at any given time. Has there ever been a bigger engineering “classroom” anywhere else? 5. Fear is not an acceptable basis for engineering. Titus believes your codebase is unsustainable if it’s not possible to make a valuable change safely. There shouldn’t be fear about making a change to a codebase. Having the right “security nets” that catch errors is strategically very valuable because it enables teams to make changes without fear. 6. With AI, outages seem to be going up. Titus talks to engineers at other companies and it’s the same picture: code output is up hugely versus a year ago, and outages are also up about 30%, while the number of features shipped is static. It seems like treading water.

articles.title: Software engineering at Google & CS education with Titus Winters
articles.headline: Google's 250M-line C++ refactoring and mandatory testing legacy
articles.summary: Titus Winters, former Google lead, details the 2010 refactoring of 250 million lines of C++ code by a team of 12 engineers. He explains how Google implemented mandatory automated testing after Search stopped shipping monthly, and discusses the scale of the company's readability program, which trained over 10,000 engineers. Winters also addresses how AI is impacting productivity and outage rates in modern software engineering.

articles.content: Genius piece of OSINT by Colsto, who demonstrates how you can take almost imperceptible background noise of planes from a video soundtrack, figure out their Doppler curves, then cross reference them against ADS-B data to find the exact location of the video based on their speed, distance, and gaps between different flights.

articles.title: I discovered a sound that leaks your exact location (and it's everywhere)
articles.headline: Researcher demonstrates how background plane noise can reveal exact video location
articles.summary: Colsto demonstrates a method to determine the exact location of a video by analyzing background plane sounds in the soundtrack. The technique involves calculating Doppler curves from plane noises, then cross-referencing them against ADS-B data using flight speed, distance, and gaps between aircraft. This OSINT technique shows how everyday video audio can leak precise geolocation data.

articles.content: Hello! Recently I needed bike lights for my bike. And I remembered that I already had rechargeable bike lights that I bought ten years ago, that I hadn’t tried in a long time. I tried to recharge them, but after fully charging them, they only worked for maybe 5 minutes before they turned off again. I don’t know much about electronics, but I’ve been curious about whether it’s possible to fix old electronics for a long time, and this seemed like the perfect repair project because I might just need to replace the battery. So I went to the local queer makerspace where I’m a member to use the soldering iron and try to do it! I don’t know much about electronics and this post does not contain any safety advice because I don’t know much about safety. I think it’s nice to do projects in a community space where you can get help. step 1: cut it open The bike light felt like it was made of silicone, so I cut open the silicone in a haphazard way along something that vaguely looked like a seam. I definitely ripped some silicone in the process and it was pretty messy but I got it open and found the circuit board. I don’t know the model number of the bike lights but there’s a photo of them at the end of the post. step 2: remove the screws There were some screws attaching things together so I removed them so I could get the circuit board out. Mostly I tried to remove as few screws as possible because I was worried about losing them or not being able to put them back after. I probably put the screws in a bag or something. step 3: get the circuit board out I took out the circuit board. Here’s what it looked like: You can see where the battery is attached, I think it’s left of RI3 and above Q2. Here’s what the battery looked like: step 4: desolder the battery I’d never desoldered anything before, so I found the iFixit guide to desoldering and read it. Also I asked my friends Lee and Lauria for advice. Here were the steps I ended up following based on the guide & the advice I got: Use a desoldering pump to remove most of the solder Once most of it is gone, kind of pull them apart to try to separate them Also try to avoid getting the battery too hot in the process by taking breaks to let it cool down. I’m not very good with a soldering iron so it took a while. The battery has an attachment that is welded to the top. For a while I thought I needed to remove this and it seemed impossible, but it turned out the replacement battery comes with that part so actually I was supposed to leave it alone. step 5: identify the battery In the picture of the battery in Step 3, you can see it says something like “3” and “LI???77”. There’s a piece of metal that I think is welded or something to the top of the battery. It seemed impossible and also maybe not smart to try to remove so I wasn’t sure how to find out what an “LI????77” was or how to order another one. I’ve been trying to avoid using LLMs (though I will not get into that because I am exhausted by LLM discourse and I’m sure you are too), but I really had no idea how to figure out what the battery was so I asked an LLM. It gave the response “LIR2477”, which (when I looked it up) looked exactly the same as my battery so I figured that was plausible. I would be interested to learn non-LLM ways to figure this out though. There must be a way. Lauria showed me how to use DigiKey’s search which was very cool though DigiKey didn’t have that part. (edit: someone in the replies told me that this kind of coin cell battery is named according to its dimensions, and you can use plastic calipers to measure the dimensions of the battery. So I guess a non-LLM way would be to measure the battery with calipers and try to match it to something on the List of battery sizes Wikipedia page, though that page only mentions CR 2477 and not LIR 2477. It’s a good example of what’s fun for me about trying to avoid LLMs, this “List of battery sizes” page is super interesting and if I use an LLM I might never find it) step 6: buy the battery I went to AliExpress and ordered: 2 batteries (I had 2 bike lights and I wanted to fix them both) some silicone glue to glue things back together I think the batteries were $3 each and the glue was $8. step 7: solder the new batteries in and glue it back together The parts took maybe 2 weeks to arive, and once they arrived, I went back to the makerspace and: soldered in the new batteries put the screws back in. The screws were very small and hard to hold, so at this point I dropped some screws on the ground and couldn’t find them because they were too small. So I just used fewer screws and hoped for the best. used the glue to try to put everything back together. Make a somewhat halfhearted attempt to clamp the parts I was gluing together Then after waiting some amount of time for the glue to dry I took it home and waited 24 hours for the glue to cure. Also I took the old batteries to somewhere nearby that accepts old batteries. it works! The lights work! I have used them to bike at night!

articles.title: Replacing the old battery on rechargeable bike lights
articles.headline: Old bike lights revived by replacing decade-old batteries
articles.summary: Julia Evans revived rechargeable bike lights purchased ten years ago by replacing the old batteries. After opening the silicone casing and removing the circuit board, Evans identified the battery type with help from an LLM and DigiKey, then ordered two replacements from AliExpress for $3 each. After soldering the new batteries in and reassembling the lights with silicone glue, the lights now function and have been used for night biking.

articles.content: Welcome back to This Week in Stratechery! As a reminder, each week, every Friday, we’re sending out this overview of content in the Stratechery bundle; highlighted links are free for everyone . Additionally, you have complete control over what we send to you. If you don’t want to receive This Week in Stratechery emails (there is no podcast), please uncheck the box in your delivery settings . On that note, here were a few of our favorites this week. Finally, Some Anthropic Numbers. Monday morning brought us Anthropic’s S-1, and not a moment too soon. After four years of arguments about the economics at frontier labs, we now have some real numbers to sink our teeth into, and Ben did just that with his Update on Tuesday . Come for that analysis, and then head over to this week’s Sharp Tech where we talked in depth about what Anthropic is telling investors, questions that remain unanswered, plus why the SEC forced Anthropic to help us understand Meta’s Muse bet . — Andrew Sharp The End of the Internet as We Know It (and I Feel Fine) . Arriving on the heels of a handful of ominous cybersecurity incidents and with continued upheaval guaranteed, Monday’s Article made two distinct predictions . First, the pressure applied by AI will eventually (or imminently?) rupture the global internet that we’ve come to know for the past 25 years. But second, as society moves to more localized solutions and products, that may in fact be a welcome development for all of us who have come to accept degraded experiences throughout our technological lives. As an avid group chatter who’s more or less abandoned public social media, I can certainly get behind the second take! — AS Autocracies Then and Now. On Sharp China this week, we began with an extended look at the climate of fear across the Chinese bureaucracy as Xi Jinping continues an anti-corruption crackdown that was absolutely necessary but may be going further than Xi’s earlier proponents ever expected. Then, we turn to a glorious mess surrounding Mao Zedong and international soccer star Kylian Mbappé. On both that episode and in this week’s Sharp Text , I make the point that connipitions like this one, anchored in a bizarre debate over Mao’s governing history, are evidence that rumors of a Chinese century have been greatly exaggerated. — AS Presented by When I write about tech companies, I am often writing about businesses that depend on Stripe , because Stripe provides the foundation for Internet-native companies — including Stratechery. Consider Substack: building Stratechery was complicated and involved gluing together disparate pieces; Substack made it easy by delivering an integrated offering. One piece that was the same, however, was Stripe: Substack creators are also Stripe customers, as are creators on many other platforms. Zoom out and the pattern repeats. Fintechs can build entire business models around card programs without ever having to build the issuing and processing infrastructure underneath it. AI companies can charge for what customers actually use, which is particularly important when usage also drives costs, without having to build the systems to track and bill for it themselves. No business succeeds because of Stripe. Stripe doesn’t answer the hard questions about what to build or whether anyone will actually use it. But it does make more things practical to try. Stratechery Articles and Updates The End of the Internet — The old Internet, where anyone could host a server is over, but it’s just the final blow in an ending that has been coming for years. The future, though, is brighter than it appears. Anthropic S-1, The Cost of Compute, Who Is Paying? — Anthropic’s IPO is finally here; the core business is very profitable, but competition may eat all of the profits, even as investors are set up for endless dilution. Meta Earnings, Muse and the Frontier, Musebook — Meta’s earnings come in the context of Zuckerberg delivering on his promise; if investors believe in Muse they must support Meta’s spending on compute. An Interview with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar About the AI Religious War — An interview with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar about AI diffusion and safety, forward-deployed engineer, and what the battle in tech is actually about. Sharp Text by Andrew Sharp Kylian Mbappés Little Red Card — Surveying the biggest scandal in China this week, and another reminder that the CCP cannot get out of its own way. Dithering with Ben Thompson and Daring Fireball’s John Gruber The End of the Internet Touchscreen MacBook Pros Asianometry with Jon Yu How Linux (and Windows) Ate UNIX Silicon Valley Walks the Jagged Edge Sharp China with Andrew Sharp and Sinocism’s Bill Bishop Five Questions on the Fifth Plenum; Mbappé Hysteria and a Chinese Own Goal; The STAR 50 AI Bubble Has Burst Greatest of All Talk The Opening Week in Review, Nuggets Darkness and Eastern Conference Angst, A True Catastrophe for OKC Sharp Tech with Andrew Sharp and Ben Thompson Anthropic Opens the Kimono, Bubble Questions and Frontier Costs, Q&A on Meta, Starlink, Brewers This week’s Stratechery video is on Do You Trust Apple? .

articles.content: Before we start: I’m in San Francisco this week and also next week. On Wed, 4 November, I’m hosting The Pragmatic Engineer Unplugged at the iconic SFJazz Club, featuring a rare conversation with Diogo Almeida (creator of Jev & co-inventor of ChatGPT), and Bryan Cantrill (cofounder and CTO of Oxide). It’s free to attend with registration, sign up here. In May 2025 at Microsoft’s annual BUILD conference, the tech giant introduced “Azure SRE Agent” with an onstage demo in which an alert fired and the AI SRE Agent went to work on identifying the root cause, and then shipped a fix, all without having to wake up a human dev oncall. Watching this demo, the whole thing felt artificial to me, and I failed to imagine any engineering team at Microsoft – or anywhere else! – letting an AI make production decisions with no human oversight that could potentially cause a worse outage. And sure enough, after last year’s BUILD I heard no more about “SRE agents” at Microsoft or elsewhere – until recently, that is. Now, I do hear it being mentioned: OpenAI built an AI SRE bot called Sevbot, and last month, an engineer at ING bank told me they’re working on their own, in-house AI SRE. Just as visibly, at tech conferences I’ve attended, AI SRE vendors’ stands have been popping up in numbers. To find out what’s going on, we reached out with Jessica to three of the most popular AI SRE startups/AI incident platforms to hear directly from them: Rootly , incident.io , and ResolveAI (note: I’m an investor in incident.io ). Thanks for all the input! Today, we cover: Why is AI SRE “hot”? Incidents and pages are trending upward, thanks to AI agents speeding up at shipping code to production. It only makes sense to invest in better oncall tooling. What does “AI SRE” mean? It’s mostly about doing incident investigation much faster, and inside of Slack. Whether “AI SREs” should make code changes is debated. Building an investigation agent. Fanning out multiple agents is common, as is the practise of engineers steering them in Slack or Teams. A “context layer” with a knowledge graph and memory is used for better investigation outcomes. Several tech companies built their own investigation agents instead of relying on vendors. Making agents accurate. Helpful approaches include verifying incident hypotheses with adversarial agents and a mix of models, as well as running evals and backtesting. However, measuring “accuracy” of AI SREs is tricky and highly specific to each company, and even engineering team. Making agents fast & affordable. Everyone wants fast, cheap, and accurate AI SREs, but there are tradeoffs. Model routing, lean prompts, and tracking cache hit rate are ways to engineer a system with the right tradeoffs for your constraints. How long until autonomous agents? The fully autonomous agents demoed on conference stages are still not a reality, but AI agents triaging pager calls – and silencing unimportant ones – is becoming more common. Interestingly, there’s not been much change in this area from how Meta operated its own systems with AI two years ago. What’s changing for on-call engineers? A new category of AI-related outages is appearing, and engineers should eventually get hit with fewer pages, but the incidents that do reach engineers will be hard. There’s a deskilling risk, and it could be smart to train oncall with incident response simulations like those from Uptime Labs . As usual, I have no affiliation with vendors mentioned in this article except for my investment in incident.io – mentioned above. I have not been paid to mention any company. 1. Why is AI SRE “hot”? A year back, there was little to no buzz about AI SREs, but that’s all been changing. The main driver seems to be that there’s a lot more code deploys. Almost all tech companies have seen their PR frequency double in a year due to AI agents. Let’s do some basic “reliability math”: i = c x p: I ncident rate = [ C hange rate] x [ P robability] C = number of changes per unit time P = probability a single change introduces failure This says that if we have few deployments (low change rate) and high confidence that each deploy works (low probability of failure), then that is a pretty stable system. But with AI agents, deploy frequency is up and the incident rate is likewise increasing at most companies. We know that C (the number of changes in a given timeframe) is up twofold or more on last year at many companies, and will probably climb higher. Data from Rootly shows that pages are also up from a year ago, and outside-business-hours pages have nearly doubled: Broadly, there’s two approaches to lowering P (incident failure rate probability): Better pre-deploy verification: more testing & verification loops Learn from incidents: make the system more resilient Most AI SRE vendors are well placed to learn from incidents and act upon them. For example, here’s Rootly’s high-level strategy for more resilient systems: 2. What does “AI SRE” mean? “AI SRE” looks on its way to becoming the agreed term for AI-augmented oncall tooling, even though we’ve not spoken to a single person who likes it – and we agree. AI SRE vendors themselves don’t like it. When we talked with incident.io, Resolve, and Rootly for this article, the reply was that, unfortunately, they’ve not come up with anything better and so this name has come to stick instead. Alternative names proved less sticky even though they’re less inaccurate, like “autonomous reliability agents”, “automated remediation agents”, and “automated incident investigation agents.” A reason “AI SRE” is less than ideal is as simple as the fact that a site reliability engineer (SRE) does a lot more than just deal with oncall alerts! They work on making a system more reliable in its entirety and a good chunk of that work happens before and after outages.

A new category of AI-related outages is emerging, with engineers facing fewer but harder-to-resolve pages. Accuracy and cost tradeoffs persist, but AI triaging and silencing unimportant alerts is becoming common, signaling a shift in on-call responsibilities.

articles.content: Gergely Orosz is frustrated at those that entered his explicitly “No AI” essay competition and used AI. He goes on to say: When I start to suspect some part is AI about someone I don’t know: how can I tell how much of it is? And how much time and effort do I want to invest to figure out? I fear most people do not realize this last part: that when it takes time and effort from others to figure out what % is AI, and what % is YOU, then I will simply assume it’s probably 100% AI and 0% you So when producing anything that is meant for other humans, if you use even a little AI, you risk the assumption that it is all AI and pointless to pay attention to In general, I agree with him, and react much the same. Once I hear LLM Voice, I flip the bozo bit and check out of the post. But as I do this I have caveats. How accurate is my neural net at AI-detection, are humans taking on AI-ish elements in their normal communication? And more seriously there are some valid uses for AI. Jim Highsmith’s story of his second brain helping him deal with Parkinson’s is one. Another is folks who don’t know English well, using AI to translate. Am I being unfair when I flip the AI voice bit when I read/listen to them? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I was sad to hear that the Grace Hopper Celebration is canceled this year. It’s an event run by Anitab.org to promote women and non-binary technologists in the software industry. Many of my colleagues have been encouraged and inspired by going to this event, which makes a refreshing change to what is often a male-dominated world. It seems the current crusade against diversity initiatives has had a big impact on funding. We are still a long way from where we should be on gender diversity in our profession, and losing an event like this only makes things more difficult. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I’ve always found Cindy Sridharan’s writing to be worth reading, and she’s broken a quiet period with a monster of an article: How to effectively debug when you no longer understand the code . Since Medium estimates it as a 64 minute read, I didn’t jump in lightly, but settled down on a flight from Amsterdam to Stuttgart. I’m glad I did, because there’s lot of good material in there, and I’d struggle to find anything to cut. In the article she uses three recent bug hunts to surface principles for how to best use an AI tool for debugging. Much of this is governed by this wise observation: Agents are not humans. They’re far more capable than humans when it comes to many things, and we should be leaning into these strengths, rather than trying to get agents to replicate human patterns of problem solving which might be suboptimal in agentic contexts. One conclusion from her experiences is that the code often isn’t the best thing for agents to look at having an agent start an investigation by first reading the code is an anti-pattern. In fact, reading the code first to formulate hypotheses about a bug should always be the very last resort of the agentic investigation process, not the starting point. An agent should first collect all available evidence about the bug, and only then formulate the hypotheses from the code that might best explain what’s being observed. She distinguishes between a bottom tier of facts: raw data that agent can find about the behavior of the system - and an upper tier of hypotheses: inferences that the agents make based on that data. Diagnosing a bug now becomes a problem of finding the hypothesis in the top tier that satisfies every fact from the bottom tier. The agents need to be steered towards the hypotheses that are the likest cause of the bug and then subject these hypotheses to validation. She has a three-step process to do this. First she identifies the most important facts, the signals that might explain or identify the bug. The factual tier has many data points. Not all of them are equally valuable. In fact, some of it might be active noise that doesn’t help an agent to be steered towards most promising hypothesis. The agent first needs to identify the data points in the factual tier that are actually related to the bug. Agents do this best when they are given a high-quality control A control is a behavior of the system that doesn’t exhibit the bug. This may be requests that trigger the bug compared to those that don’t, or different builds of the product, or the same build in different environments. With signals highlighted, she then focuses on the hypotheses that are most promising, because they fit best with the signals. A hypothesis should satisfy all the facts, the most valuable signals are those that are only satisfied by a few hypotheses. A table of hypotheses and signals helps visualize the strength of the signals and the likelihood of the hypotheses. The third step is then validating the promising hypotheses against every fact, treating each fact as constraint on the solution. Across the three bugs chronicled in this post, my most valuable contributions weren’t knowledge of the code. They were picking a control, choosing a constraint, and rejecting a hypothesis that hadn’t been validated. The engineers who thrive in an agent-native world will be the ones who are good at designing such verification loops, whether or not they understand the code it verifies. This directing has to remember the opening point that agents have different capabilities to humans. A human wants to deal with less data. All abstractions we currently have (aggregation, visualizations etc) are designed to help humans deal with less data.
