articles.content: Release: llm 0.37 There's a lot of stuff in this new release of my LLM CLI tool and Python library, representing around two months of accumulated features and fixes. I added gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-6.1-terra , plus a new llm openai endpoint add command to make it easier to configure additional models that use OpenAI-compatible endpoints. I switched the default model (if you have not set your own default) to gpt-6-luna - half the price of the previous default, gpt-5.6-luna . LLM's support for embeddings now accepts that different binary content may have different content-type - necessary for models like Gemini Embedding 2 , which can embed text, audio, images, and video. A lot of open source maintainers complain about a flood of AI-assisted PRs. LLM is my project that has been most affected by this and, to be honest, I'm not finding it to be a problem. That's mainly because I have Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra help me with triage to spot the most useful fixes! This release includes fixes from 12 authors - almost all AI-assisted - and the burden of reviewing them wasn't nearly as great as I expected. I really see them as bug reports with attached examples - sometimes I land them, sometimes I implement my own fix. So thanks to 0d00ciallo0721 , ac1982 , Allen Flux , Bian Yuhan , Bishop Kammeraad , Chen Yufeiyang , Christopher Krah , Ethan Stoner , Jiachen Xie , Olamide Faniyan , Sharat Chandra Sai Boddu , nosmile99 for helping out with (or spending tokens on) this release!

articles.content: Listen to this post: Good morning, Today’s Stratechery Interview is with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar . Sankar has worked at Palantir for 20 years, and has taken on an increasingly visible role as public intellectual, including authoring the book Mobilize , an exhortation “To Reboot the American Industrial Base and Stop World War III”. I previously interviewed Sankar in June 2023 . That interview is a great place to start in terms of understanding Palantir, which we mostly discuss in this interview in the context of AI. To that end, in this interview we discuss why Sankar thinks the industry is insufficiently focused on AI diffusion, why companies focused on the top-line have more success adopting AI, and why he is frustrated at the labs refusal to take a systems engineering approach to AI safety. Then we discuss what Palantir has learned from AI, how companies can preserve alpha instead of the median, and whether or not we need more models. Sankar also explains exactly what a forward-deployed engineer is, why tech is in a religious war, and his retrospective on Anthropic’s battle with the U.S. government. This Interview is presented by Stripe, the economic infrastructure of AI, and for Stratechery itself. As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player. On to the Interview: An Interview with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar About the AI Religious War This interview is lightly edited for clarity. Topics: Diffusing Intelligence | Top Line vs. Bottom Line | Safety and Systems Engineering | Palantir’s AI Lessons | Alpha vs. Beta | Model Questions | Forward-Deployed Engineering | Anthropic vs. the U.S. Government | AI Religion Background Shyam Sankar, welcome back to Stratechery. SS: Ben, thanks for having me back. Well, the last time we talked was in conjunction with Ted Mabrey , the head of Palantir Commercial. As is usually the case with dual interviews, we got right down to business — and I do have to say, I do a lot of interviews where I usually kind of know where I want to go, but that one was super helpful to me in understanding Palantir and thinking about AI generally . But before we get into that, we never got to do my traditional background questions — where you came from, how you got to where you are. So for you, do we start in Orlando, in Lagos, or in India? SS: At least Lagos. My father, in his early 20s, moved to Lagos and built one of the first pharmaceutical manufacturing facilities in all of Africa. He set up this whole life there for the better part of ten years. I was born in India, but really I grew up until I was three in Lagos. And then there was this horrible armed robbery that happened at the house — they decapitated the dog, pistol-whipped my father, and threatened my mother. So we left all of our earthly possessions behind and started over again in Orlando, which ended up being a truly phenomenal place to grow up. The profound optimism of Disney World, the shadow of the Space Coast , seeing shuttle launches in elementary school, running into your courtyard filled with this sense of optimism about how technology will inevitably lead to a better world — which, if you fast-forward twenty years from the ’80s, I think kids were fed a very different diet of Terminator and “ nature always finds a way “, “How dare man try to do anything that creates progress?”, so that’s really where it started. Is that actually the ultimate example of man overcoming nature — not the space shuttle, but in fact Disney World? SS: (laughing) That’s true! The fact that millions of people go there every year, to the middle of the swamp — and it’s fantastic, a lot of fun. What does meritocracy mean to you? I was reading the recent profile of you in Colossus , and it opened with [Palantir CEO] Alex Karp’s statements in that regard, but it was put in the context of you growing up in Orlando, taking an entrance exam to go to Trinity High School, and how that launched you into what you became. Is that a sentiment from Alex, is it from you, or what’s your take? SS: It’s a sentiment for both of us, for different reasons. We’re both kind of acquired tastes, in many ways, and living in a world that judges you by the fruits you bear, rather than any dimension you have no control over, is obviously a better world to live in. I think it’s a precondition to the American Dream. I was going to ask you that. Because you have this background — born in India, originally living in Lagos, come to America. What does being an American mean to you? Is that the same question, or is there some tension between those two things? SS: They overlap profoundly. Being an American is this profound belief in your own human agency, and the community you’re in, and the ability to create a more perfect union — the recognition, the ability to hold the contradiction, that not everything is perfect today but it’s incumbent on us to make it better. That may sound a little Pollyannish and even corny, but that doesn’t exist anywhere else. Everywhere else, people are profoundly cynical — things are the way they are — and there’s a very thin line between cynicism and nihilism, and you kind of give up on everything. That’s the death spiral, that’s how you get the Dark Ages. After university and graduate school, you worked on Xoom, on remittances — and then you go to work for Palantir. SS: Xoom with an X. Xoom with an X, that’s right.

articles.headline: Team modernizes 800,000 battery-powered IoT sensors across 3,000 stores
articles.summary: A team modernized a large IoT fleet of 800,000 battery-powered sensors across 3,000 stores, moving to newer connectivity technology without replacing existing devices. They built a physical IoT lab and sensor farm to experiment with radio behavior and power consumption, designed diagnostics and remote interfaces into device firmware, and created a virtual device emulator to simulate large-scale network limits. Key practices included treating hardware as part of the development environment, designing devices to explain themselves, and carefully designing for intermittent connectivity and limited energy. The effort replaced reasonable assumptions with sensible defaults for large-scale deployment.

articles.content: I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies , a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis , and then to experiment with Claude's new Code Interpreter . I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of Executive Order 14434 , aka the asinine Super Intelligence one. First, the updated chart Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total - the surveyed group (a "panel") cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks. The latest data is published on alternating Thursdays at 10am. I used the most recent numbers (published October 22, 2026) to create a new version ( GPT-6 Astra Extra High transcript ) of the AI adoption chart, updated to reflect both the last twelve months and a change that was made to the survey question sent out by the Bureau: Here's a link to the larger image . For comparison, here's that AI adoption chart from last year (my GPT-5 version): In September 2025 the largest (250+ employees) companies answered "yes" around 12% of the time to the question about whether they used AI in "producing goods or services". Under the new "any business function" wording, by February 2026, those same large companies answered "yes" around 30% of the time, and by October 2026 that had increased to around 40%. The data in the above chart comes from the "Employment size class" XLSX file, available from here . Here's a copy of the file I used. You can view the survey document that is sent out to businesses - here's my snapshot copy of that 346KB PDF. The changing language of the questions As the chart demonstrates, the question asked by the Bureau changed in a material way on November 17th, 2025. Prior to that date, the question they asked was this (emphasis mine): In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in producing goods or services ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) On December 3rd, 2025, the Bureau announced a significant change to that question. Here's the replacement: In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in any of its business functions ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) No more "producing goods or services" - now it's "in any of its business functions"! This means that the answers to the question before and after November 17th are not directly comparable. From October 19, 2026, they ask about Super Intelligence When I went looking for the updated question language in the latest XLSX file, I couldn't find it. I found this instead: In the last two weeks, did this business use Super Intelligence or SI (formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of SI use include: SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service; SI-powered forecasting or pricing; SI-driven computer vision for quality control, etc.) The BTOS about page explains what happened: Beginning with the October 19, 2026 collection, instrument wording was updated due to Executive Order 14434 . The current numbers reflect the old Artificial Intelligence survey wording - the first survey results reflecting the Super Intelligence wording are due for publication on Thursday. Is this going to affect the survey? The obvious open question here is whether this wording change is going to affect the survey results. The businesses answering this survey will have last seen that question twelve weeks ago, when it was still called AI. Hopefully the new language isn't going to confuse them, especially since the survey helpfully spells out "formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI". I can't help but laugh at the absurdity of "SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service" though.

articles.title: The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”
articles.headline: Census Bureau renames AI to 'Super Intelligence' in business survey
articles.summary: The U.S. Census Bureau updated its Business Trends and Outlook Survey question language in November 2025, replacing 'producing goods or services' with 'any business function'. Effective October 19, 2026, the survey was renamed to reference 'Super Intelligence' per Executive Order 14434. This wording change makes historical data incomparable, with large company AI adoption rates jumping from 12% to 30-40% due to the broader question scope rather than actual adoption growth.

articles.content: Before we start: I’m very excited to announce an The Pragmatic Engineer Unplugged live event: with Diogo Almeida (the creator of Jev) and Bryan Cantrill (cofounder and CTO, Oxide). 4 November (Wednesday), San Francisco, the SFJAZZ Center. It’s free to attend, but spaces are limited and registration is required . Stream the latest episode Listen and watch now on YouTube , Apple , and Spotify . See the episode transcript at the top of this page, and timestamps for the episode at the bottom. Brought to You by • turbopuffer – vector and full-text search built on object storage: fast, 10x cheaper, and extremely scalable. Under the hood, the team are rewriting the tpuf storage engine. Follow along until it hits production at turbopuffer.com/v3 • What if you only needed a single test to harden your system? Get a free introduction to property-based testing : through a live, online webinar hosted by Hillel Wayne (a recent podcast guest ), author of Logic for Programmers and Developer Educator at Antithesis. RSVP here . • Entire – Git hosting, rebuilt for the agentic era. Entire hosts your code in-region, and is up to 89x faster than any other competitor. Mirror from GitHub with a single click – I’ve already done so. In this episode What’s changed in “the unwritten rules” of engineering management since the 2010s, why are hands-on managers “back”, and what has it done to the engineer-to-CTO career path? Today’s guest is one of the best people I know who can tackle these questions. Will Larson is CTO of Imprint , was an engineering executive for 10+ years, and is the author of several popular books on engineering leadership, including ‘ The Engineering Executive’s Primer ,’ ‘ Staff Engineer , An Elegant Puzzle ,’ and ‘ Crafting Engineering Strategy .’ Previously, he was also CTO at Carta and Calm, and an engineering leader at Stripe and Uber. In this episode, we explore how engineering leadership has evolved from management practices shaped in the long post-financial-crisis ZIRP era to the altered expectations of engineers and managers today. Is middle management an increasingly precarious career path, and might managers need to reskill and return to hands-on technical work – or even consider retirement? Will makes the case, and we hear why the traditional path to engineering executive roles is changing, as well as why taking one step backward might sometimes be the best way forward. We discuss Will’s early career, and get his first-hand account of Digg’s disastrous relaunch, his own path to CTO, and he tells us why career ladders still matter. We also explore how AI is changing engineering roles and bringing technical decision-making back to leadership. Takeaways from the conversation with Will Here are some standout talking points from our conversation, during which Will recommends middle managers to go back to line management and re-skill like he has done. He didn’t ask me to, but I want to mention that he’s hiring for several key engineering manager roles at Imprint to use agents to rethink how software teams work. 1. Will shares an inside account of how a 10 website sank into irrelevance after a v4 rewrite. Digg was the “king” of social media sites in the late 2000s; bigger than Reddit, and one of top-10 most visited websites, globally. That all crashed to a halt in 2010 when the company embarked on a massive rewrite called Digg v4 – and it was a disaster. It was the start of Digg’s downfall. Will worked at Digg during this rewrite, and shares how Digg was already losing traction and traffic to Facebook, and that Google changed its algorithm which caused 60-70% traffic loss. From the outside, Digg looked like it was growing, but its business prospects were shrinking fast. The company had about 120 people and was burning through money fast. Into this entered the v4 rewrite, which was carried out to a hard deadline set by Kevin Rose, the newly-returned CEO at the time. The v4 version alienated passionate users, and had major performance and reliability problems. Will and a small engineering team fixed the issues. The root cause was Python memory leaks introduced by devs who didn’t know Python so well. Will has shared more detail on his blog . Even so, Will doesn’t think the rewrite killed Digg: with or without that rewrite, Digg would’ve met the same fate of being overtaken and replaced by Facebook and Reddit. 2. At Yahoo, a “black market” for servers popped up after the cofounder insisted on personally approving new servers. A hilarious story of how incentives drive behavior: Yahoo cofounder, David Filo, wanted to drive accountability by teams justifying every server purchase. This created a “black” market and Will recalled that one engineer on his team had 30 servers left from a canceled project that he traded with devs who could not get approvals elsewhere, in exchange for stuff he needed. Also, servers didn’t have to be returned, so Yahoo ended up running a large number of outdated, power-hungry machines! 3. In the 2000s, having annual 1:1s with managers was normal. Will worked at Yahoo in 2008-2010 and had two 1:1 sessions with his manager: one in which they asked Will about someone else’s performance, and the next one when he handed in his notice after it finished. It was pretty common for 1:1s with managers to be rare things at the time. 4. Too many Staff+ engineers only want to work on fun problems. At Stripe, Will led an org of about 250 people, where lots of the most senior engineers regularly sought more “engaging” problems to work on. Will eventually found his optimal response: “I only have suffering to offer, but this suffering is what’s going to make the business succeed.” However, he felt that he was seen by some as guilty of violating an unwritten rule of management by not finding enough – or interesting enough – problems for them to engage with.

articles.content: I've been getting the occasional confusing Python dependency error since switching over to Python 3.15 and the rule I'm having to remember is: If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file Most of my projects are libraries which don't include a uv.lock file, since it's rude for a library dependency to lock versions for anything else that uses it. Running uv run pytest etc tends to leave uv.lock files lying around, which are listed in .gitignore and so do not get committed to my repositories. But... sometimes that uv.lock pins a version of a dependency that doesn't yet have a Python 3.15 wheel. An example from earlier today: error: Failed to build `watchfiles==1.1.1` cause: Call to `maturin.build_wheel` failed error: the configured Python interpreter version (3.15) is newer than PyO3's maximum supported version (3.14) Deleting that file and running uv run pytest again usually fixes the problem.

articles.headline: Python 3.15 users delete uv.lock to fix dependency errors

Deleting the lock file and re-running tests typically resolves the issue, particularly for library projects that do not normally include uv.lock.

articles.content: A software engineer whose company is looking into its own spending on AI tools pinged me with a very timely question recently, asking what other companies spend on AI, per engineer. They were also keen to find out what the PR throughput was before and after the spending on AI at other places. Spending on AI agents is ballooning at all the tech companies I talk with this year. With 2027 coming around fast, many companies are seeking to put a realistic number on how much they really spend on AI. The change in PR throughput is a very simple metric, and one of those “readily-available” measurements at nearly all companies, It’s also one that probably has not been “gamed” by devs yet, and it’s possible to compare a “before AI” and “after AI” measurement with this metric. To find out more and to try and answer the reader’s question, I asked around and got to talk with engineering leaders and senior+ engineers at 27 workplaces. I also gathered aggregate data from CodeRabbit and Gitar. This article summarizes what I found, covering: Stats from CodeRabbit and Gitar. Weekly PRs by devs using the AI code review tool increased by around 2x compared to a year ago. Meanwhile, Gitar sees “AI-native” teams ship 60+ PRs/dev/week. AI spending patterns of 27 companies. Spending caps are common, and there’s no connection between company size and AI spend. High spenders ($1,000+ per month). A quant shop has seen AI costs increase 15x since January, while a two-person .NET shop spends $3,000/dev/month, plus details from six more companies. AI spend at Big Tech. Meta and NVIDIA encourage devs to use AI heavily, while engineers at Apple are far more cautious. Medium spenders . Details from five companies spending $300-500/month/dev. Low spenders . Companies spending below $300/month/dev, many of which use subsidized subscriptions. Including details from a publicly traded company, a nonprofit, fintech Lendscape (UK), and startups Lonestone (France), Paulina24 (Germany) and 5 others. What’s the ROI of AI? A question that few companies seem able to answer – at least for now. 1. Stats from CodeRabbit and Gitar The team at CodeRabbit polled data engineers using the platform, anonymized it, and has kindly shared it with us. They saw a 113% increase in weekly PRs: There’s a 127% rise in monthly PRs: When tracking the same group of 20,000 developers, the increase is nearly identical across the platform: a 128% increase: Across customer groups, there seems to be “tiers” of PR frequency. Here’s data from Gitar (Sonar’s AI code verification agent) on PRs/week/dev across hundreds of customers: I suspect that a lot has to do with company culture: whenever you join a new team, you pick up the pace pretty quickly. If the company is one where ~5 PRs per week is considered a high output, then new joiners get used to that pace. If it’s a place where most people ship 20-30 PRs to production per week, then new joiners pick up that pace! 2. AI Spending patterns of 27 companies I got details on AI spending and changes in the rate of PRs from 27 different companies. I anonymized most names by request. At a glance, here’s how spend looks like: A few common themes from this data set: Company size and spend on AI are unrelated. In the data set, a 2-person .NET startup spends $3,000/month/dev, and a publicly traded company with 1,500 engineers, limits devs to $150 of AI spend per month. Spend peaked during the summer, and is falling. June and July saw peak monthly spend at nearly all companies, and costs have roughly halved for those on API plans. A mix of Opus 5.5 and moving to open models is the reason for the drop at most companies. Spending caps are common at medium-and-above spenders. It’s normal to have a spending cap in place at medium-and-above spenders, where additional spend needs to be justified. Most people say the caps are easily avoided. Subscriptions conceal concrete AI costs, but some subsidies are ending. Several companies mentioned that their subsidized AI subscriptions are coming to an end, so they need to prepare to either optimize costs, or have their bill increase 5-10x. Claude and Opus 5.5 seem to be the favorite models. Within this rather limited data, Claude and Opus 5.5 dominated answers about where most of the spending goes. Cursor, Codex and GitHub Copilot were also mentioned. 3. High spenders ($1,000+ per month) Here are details of companies spending considerable amounts each month on AI coding tools. Quant trading shop, ~5,000 staff (circa 2,000 devs) This company has seen its AI spend balloon overall: total spend was $8M /month in September, a 16x increase on the $500K/month spend in January! The average spend is $1,600 /dev/month (up from around $80 in January). Most are going to Claude, and the biggest spenders are not devs, but traders. A current engineer there told me: “Lots of traders are using Claude. Engineering is learning the importance of rate limiting for traders who accidentally run expensive queries without realizing it.” The company has a $25,000 limit per employee for AI, which is extremely high, more than at NVIDIA! The engineer explained this generous limit: “The last few years have, generally, been extremely profitable for trading firms. For us, last year was our most profitable year ever – and we’re already on track to beat it this year. So, the spend on AI is well within what these companies can afford.” AI outlay is expected to grow: this firm is building its own internal GPU and CPU farms to run models, and are building models expected to beat state-of-the-art (SOTA) models like Fable, according to their own data. ROI is measured differently at trading firms. The ROI of any spend is the profit or loss made by a trading desk, and AI spend is now part of the costbase. So, provided the desk’s profit increases, no questions are expected.

articles.summary: Engineering leaders at 27 workplaces report that AI spending caps are common at medium-to-high spenders, with subsidized subscriptions ending and costs potentially increasing 5-10x. Weekly PRs via AI code review tools increased around 2x year-over-year, while 'AI-native' teams ship 60+ PRs per developer weekly. High spenders include a quant shop with 16x cost increase since January and a .NET shop at $3,000 per developer monthly. Meta and NVIDIA encourage heavy AI use, while Apple engineers remain cautious. Companies struggle to measure ROI as AI costs balloon across varying spend levels.

articles.content: Naresh Jain compares coding agents building the same API service with and without a behavioral harness. A frontier model, GPT-6 Sol, passed every external evaluation either way. But a cost-optimized model, GPT-6 Luna, succeeded in only 3 of 10 unharnessed runs and all 10 with the harness. While adding the harness increased token usage and runtime for Luna, the harnessed Luna runs achieved the same 10-for-10 reliability as GPT-6 Sol while costing 33% less per run ($0.273 vs $0.406). This experiment suggests a behavioral harness might be a practical way to get dependable results from smaller, cost-optimized models. more…

The experiment compared coding agents building a backend-for-frontend service with and without the harness, finding the harness provides dependable results from smaller models.

articles.content: Stream the latest episode Listen and watch now on YouTube , Apple , and Spotify . See the episode transcript at the top of this page, and timestamps for the episode at the bottom. Brought to You by • turbopuffer – The turbopuffer engineering team is doing something really cool: they are completely redesigning their storage architecture from first principles to make search faster, cheaper, and more reliable at scale. And they’re documenting all of it! Follow along their rewrite at turbopuffer.com/v3 • Linear – one of the big challenges for us devs is the sheer amount of code to review. Linear Diffs is a new feature to review PRs inside of Linear, with all the context in one place. It even supports stacked PRs. Check it out • WorkOS – how do you deal with agents and permissions? WorkOS built Airlock , the authorization layer for AI agents. It evaluates every request against the agent’s intent and your rules and either allows it, denies it, or routes it to a human for approval. Works with Claude Code, Codex and MCP gateways. Give it a spin In this episode What do developer tools look like inside Uber, today? They are very different from what you would see at most places. For example, can you guess what service a system called DevPods, Code Inbox, Slate or Wisdom would be providing to engineers? Today’s episode is a deepdive into the day-to-day tools of devs at Uber, our tour guide being on of Uber’s longest-tenured engineers: Uday Kiran Medisetty . Uday is one of the few Distinguished Engineers at the company, and leads much of the work on agentic AI, today. With Uday, we talk through how Uber’s developer infrastructure prepared it for AI agents. We look at the systems Uber built before generative AI and the new tools that connect agents to its code, internal services, and engineering knowledge. Uday explains how engineers use background agents, why tools like Slate make development (and bugfixing!) more efficient, and how code review is changing. We also cover Uber’s approach to token costs and how it measures productivity as the engineer’s role changes. Takeaways from the conversation with Uday Here are 11 interesting learnings from today’s episode: 1. Uber’s service count changed erratically: in 2015, when Uday joined, there were two services in total. By 2019, there were thousands. In 2026, there will be about the same number of services than in 2019, even though the business is about 10x larger than back then! 2. Uber built most services in-house because off-the-shelf software could not handle its scale – or simply did not exist! Examples of services Uber built because it had to: uOwn : shows who owns a service or asset. Back in 2015, no such vendor existed. M3DB : Uber was emitting about 500 million metrics per second, with no vendor being able to handle this load, so they built it themselves. Observability company Chronosphere was built on top of the open sourced M3DB, and we previously covered how Uber built its observability platform . Cadence : a durable workflow engine for multi-day flows like driver onboarding. No such system existed at the time when Uber needed it. Temporal was built on top of the open sourced Cadence framework. Morpheus : a system combining feature flags and experimentation, including switchback tests, with support for two- and three-sided marketplaces that Uber operates. Again, no such solution existed when Uber needed it. 3. At Uber, cities are a first-class concept that go all the way down to physical infrastructure. Another reason Uber had to build a lot of its custom tooling is how the concept of cities is a “basic primitive” that needs to be handled across systems like observability, feature flagging, deployments, and even service sharding. For example, in the early days, some services had their database sharded by cities. Even today, each city is pinned to a cloud region, and can fall over to another region at any time. We previously covered how Uber moved from bare metal to the cloud . 4. A single AI model gateway has paid lots of dividends. In 2023, Uber’s platform team made the decision that everything built with AI needs to be model- and harness-agnostic. They built Model Gateway to support switching between Anthropic, OpenAI, other vendor models, and now also supports open models they run. Having the Model Gateway in place made it easy to extend with these parts: AI Guard : a middleware run by the security team. It checks all requests and responses, and measures latencies (and flags overly slow models or queries) Spend tracking: spend is tracked per user Visibility : audit logs and session traces 5. AIFX allows engineers to switch harnesses without losing settings. Uber currently supports Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode as harnesses. AIFX (short for AI Foundations) is a wrapper on top of all of these, so when an engineer changes harnesses, all their settings, skills and plugins move with them. 6. Uber has a hybrid approach to AI spend: engineers get allocated a spend tier. When they hit the limit, their manager can sign off to spend more in that month. Basically, for the right type of work, there is no spend limit, but Uber doesn’t want engineers to carelessly burn tokens. A plugin called CostCheck works across sessions and gives tips on how to improve an engineer’s cost profile. Uber has reduced token costs by about 50% the last few months, as we previously covered. 7. All PRs are still reviewed by engineers, but Uber built tools to help devs decide how much time they need to spend on each code change. Uday admits that code review has become a big bottleneck inside the company, and Uber built Code Review to make it easier and more efficient for devs to do these reviews.

articles.content: In response to my last fragments (probably the bit about us worrying if LLMs have consciousness when we when we should be wondering why they don’t have a conscience) “Metalanguage” replied : we shipped the id and forgot the superego. classic software lifecycle. I don’t know what was on their mind, but their post immediately made me think of the classic 1956 movie Forbidden Planet. Plenty of sci-fi, and other literature, have explored humans creating technology with unintended behavior, going back at least to Mary Shelly. But that movie was particularly influential on sci-fi film-making and in the heart of its story is what happens when we nurture a thinking machine. I use the term “nurture” here deliberately. We talk of building software, but building implies a degree of determinism. When we build a bridge, or a locomotive, we expect it to behave in a controlled and well-understood manner. That’s a difference in degree to how we cultivate plants in our garden, or nurture young children. One of the challenges of working with these systems is understanding what has changed in this shift from building a computational system to nurturing an inferential one, and how our processes need to change in response. We get unintended behavior with deterministic building: some bridges have collapsed, and our computational systems often have bugs. But one difference is that when we find a bug in a computational system we can usually fix it. Even if we can’t, we can usually disable a component so the bug won’t do further harm. With inferential LLMs however, there is no such simple fix or disablement, which may lead us to the fate of the Krell. (If you haven’t seen Forbidden Planet, it’s well worth watching. Yes, it shows it was made in the 1950s - with special effects, music, acting, and attitudes of that decade. But the story is solid, and its key theme is very relevant to the future we build with generative AI. Just don’t read about it in advance, it’s better to be immersed in the story without spoilers - although my memory of that experience is understandably hazy.) ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Many people who follow me also know my friend Ola Bini, who was my colleague at Thoughtworks for many years, and was living in Ecuador working as an independent software security expert. Sadly his time in Ecuador was dogged by a bogus prosecution by the authorities there. But things seemed to have settled down, and although not allowed to leave Ecuador, Ola was able to get on with his life. Sadly that’s no longer the case as he was deported from Ecuador on Friday: According to information released by his lawyer, Bini was intercepted by a car with four people who identified themselves as immigration agents. He was then taken to an immigration office without further information or a formal order from a competent authority. There, officials told Bini that his visa had been revoked but didn’t show any supporting document. Bini’s defense filed a habeas corpus to safeguard his freedom and prevent his deportation. Yet, Ecuadorian authorities affirmed that the developer represents a threat or risk to public security and the state structure, and must leave the country. The ground for deportation is a secret report which allegedly asserts that Bini committed acts against the security of Ecuador. The defense could not access its contents. I was really worried for a while, since it wasn’t clear where he was going to be deported to. But he tweeted from Sweden , so I’m thankful for that. But this is only a partial relief. Ola has spent thirteen years in Ecuador and made it his home. To be thrown out of your home for scant reason is a heavy thing to bear, and the officials who did that have committed a serious offense. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ DDD Europe have released the video of Gien Verschatse interviewing Eric Evans and myself at the conference in June. We start by talking about how we bonded over conceptual modeling in the late 1990s. The conversation quickly moves to AI, we note that it’s impossible to predict how such a big change will work out. We do expect that it will cause us to think about our work in different ways, but the change may well be liberating, it’s reinvigorated Eric’s love of programming. people are probably going to feel very frustrated by [the new way of thinking about software]… but when you get through that, there is a kind of a wonderful feeling of my brain’s been loosened up. Our background in agile planning helps with the uncertainty, as we are used to taking small steps and being attentive to feedback. We mull on the interplay of writing and thinking, in terms of both prose and code, and how its very much an iterative process of exploration and refinement - the same is true when we chat with our LLMs. And don’t miss Eric’s important final tip. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Paul Graham: There were a lot of things that only worked because there’s a limit to the rate at which humans can operate. We’re about to find out what all of them are, as they break. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ The speculation continues about whether or not reading code will play a part in a software developer’s future. Geoffrey Huntley says . People are still saying, very loudly, that code should be readable so that humans can understand it. I no longer think that’s the goal. Interestingly his example has the LLM explain a haskell function definition… by translating it to Python. Which, to me, suggests there is a role for code - just that LLM need not store code in the same form that it presents it to a reader. This is essentially the same idea as projectional editing , which posits that the editable representation of software need not be the same as its storage representation.

articles.title: Fragments: October 4
articles.headline: Fowler warns inferential AI lacks simple fixes for unintended behavior
articles.summary: Martin Fowler contrasts building deterministic software with nurturing inferential AI systems, noting that bugs in traditional code can usually be fixed or disabled, while LLMs present no such simple remedy. He references the 1956 film Forbidden Planet as a cautionary tale about nurturing thinking machines. Fowler also discusses Ola Bini's deportation from Ecuador, arguing the secret security report lacks transparency. Additionally, he explores how AI is reshaping software development, suggesting coding roles are changing rather than disappearing, and that higher-level representations are needed to manage token limits in LLM contexts.

articles.content: Last week’s guest on the podcast was Sam Newman , who had released a book I’ve personally long awaited titled Building Resilient Distributed Systems . It’s an especially timely book for many of us software engineers, as we’re seeing more outages with nearly all services and systems – much of it caused by more code deploys thanks to AI agents writing more code; and more bugs causing more incidents in production. Sam’s book being “fresh out of the oven,” it naturally also touches on what AI changes as we design resilient systems. In fact, Sam told me that he took a total of three years to finished the book – instead of the two he originally planned – because he went back and reworked all parts of the book, updating parts where AI is relevant to talk about. I asked Sam if he would consider sharing an excerpt from the book, with sections especially relevant for anyone building systems that ought to be reliable. Sam graciously agreed, and today’s issue covers a few important topics, spread across two chapters from his book. We get into: Disaster recovery (DR). Recovering from catastrophic failures: planning for cloud region/data center/site-wide outages, the concept of RPO and RTO, DRO objectives and SLOs. Disaster Recovery Patterns. Backup-and-restore, pilot light failover, warm failover and multisite active-active. Infrastructure availability when planning for DR. Ongoing GPU and CPU shortages mean you cannot expect infrastructure availability at all times, so you need to understand constraints your vendors have, and to prioritize critical services. Resiliency of AI-powered software. Model provider resilience, the challenge of models changing, and the need for observability. How to handle uncertainty. Tactics like being multi-model and multi-vendor, making costs transparent, and frequently analyzing vendors. Even though this article is pretty long, we cover less than a full chapter from the book's 16 chapters. If you build reliable systems for a living, I warmly recommend the book itself, and you can get it from the publisher . My usual disclaimer: as with all my recommendations, I was not paid to recommend this book, and none of the links are affiliate ones. See my ethics statement for more details. The excerpts below are from Building Resilient Distributed Systems , by Sam Newman. Copyright © 2026 Sam Newman. Published by O’Reilly Media, Inc. Used with permission. 1. Disaster Recovery Excerpt from Chapter 10: Disaster Recovery. We’ve already discussed how to handle a variety of failures that impact individual service instances. But what happens when a catastrophic failure causes widespread outage of large parts of your system? Fire, flood, electrical supply issues, and errors in the underlying cloud infrastructure are all outside of your control, and at one fell swoop, they can render your attempts to make your system more robust totally redundant. Handling these situations falls under the auspices of disaster recovery (DR), a set of procedures that should kick in when something really bad happens. As with much of what we’ve looked at in this book, trade-offs abound. As you reduce your period of acceptable downtime or data loss, cost and complexity increase, so picking the right approach for your system can be a delicate balancing act. In this chapter, I’ll give you some concrete targets to work with to help drive your own DR approach. Cloud Region, Data Center, or Site? The exact terminology you use to discuss your infrastructure will likely vary based on implementation details, and this in turn can make discussions around generally applicable patterns more difficult. When running on the public cloud, for example, you’ll probably be familiar with the concept of a cloud region, which is where your cloud resources live. When running on a private cloud or in a more traditional on-premises setup, you’ll instead think in terms of data centers. As we discuss the various options around handling DR, the patterns that we’ll see later in this chapter can be used for either public or private cloud scenarios. Therefore, to keep things simple, I’ll use the term site as a general descriptor of where your computing infrastructure lives. There are some specific issues to consider around mixing cloud vendors as part of a DR strategy, and we’ll look more at those in Chapter 11. How Good Does Your DR Need to Be? A spectrum of DR options are available to you, and they can range greatly in terms of cost, complexity, and recovery. To help you decide which DR approach is most appropriate, we should first try to understand how to determine the appropriate requirements for your context. A simple way to define technical requirements around DR is to make use of two concrete measurable targets, recovery point objective and recovery time objective. In Figure 10-1, you can see how these objectives relate to an incident: Recovery Point Objective The recovery point objective (RPO) defines the maximum amount of time that can have passed since the data was last backed up or synchronized. Put another way, RPO defines the upper duration of potential data loss. If the data for your system backs up once an hour, then it’s possible to lose up to an hour of data if your system has an incident. Therefore, your RPO would be an hour. Recovery Time Objective The recovery time objective (RTO) defines how long it’s acceptable for your system to be unavailable in the wake of an incident. If all your computers became unavailable, perhaps because of a data center–wide outage, how long would it take you to have your services running in an alternative data center? Your RTO includes all the time needed to recover data from the last recovery point, make computing resources available for your workloads, and redirect traffic to your new site—so there are more variables to consider in terms of bringing your system back online than just time.

articles.title: Principles for effective slides
articles.headline: Fowler outlines principles for effective presentation slides
articles.summary: Martin Fowler and Sumeet explain that slides should complement, not replace, the speaker. Key principles include controlling the rate of knowledge exposition, tight coupling between visuals and speech, minimalism by default, and avoiding sending slides in advance. Effective slides use visuals to reinforce the narrative without repeating spoken content, ensuring the audience focuses on the message rather than reading ahead.

articles.content: A Sensible Default is a practice that, absent some overriding context, should be used when carrying out a certain kind of task. In software development such sensible defaults might include things like “use version control”, “separate UI logic from domain logic”, “automate deployment pipelines”. The term “sensible default” is a deliberate contrast to “best practice”. Folks dislike calling things “best practice” because that term implies a general presumption that the best practice is something we should always expect to do. A “sensible default”, however, is something that should be reassessed in a new context, something that can (and should) be overridden when circumstances change. I first heard the term when it was popularized within Thoughtworks by Evan Bottcher. He got the name from talking to James Ross, and found the phrasing appealing as carried the nuance he was seeking, a known-good starting point. A sensible default is what we'd expect you to do, the practices to apply, if there are no hard constraints in the environment. Do these practices, or do better, and be prepared to explain why you've chosen some other way. -- Evan Bottcher Thoughtworks has since made much of this concept, including publishing a playbook of the ones we use. We expect people to be familiar with these defaults, ready to use them when starting any new piece of work. They are our defaults because we've used them in many situations and found them to be effective. But teams should also be familiar with their limitations, and able to judge whether they should be changed depending on the particular circumstances. As the twelfth agile principle says: “At regular intervals, the team reflects on how to become more effective, then tunes and adjusts its behavior accordingly.” We also reassess these defaults regularly - this is the heart of the Thoughtworks Technology Radar . Searching on the web led me to a post from Steve Bennett on Sensible Defaults . The post was written at about the time Evan talked to James. I do not know whether it was where James got the name from, or whether it appeared in parallel.

articles.title: Bliki: Sensible Default
articles.headline: Thoughtworks popularizes 'sensible default' practice in software development
articles.summary: Thoughtworks has embraced 'sensible defaults' as a software development practice, contrasting with 'best practice' by allowing context-specific overrides. The concept, popularized by Evan Bottcher, includes defaults like using version control and automating deployment pipelines. Teams are expected to follow these practices unless circumstances require change, reflecting the agile principle of regular reflection and adjustment.
